speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in spite of the natural enthusiasm which members are expressing in meeting here for the first time, I should like to move a motion under Standing Order 43 with regard to a matter of urgent and pressing importance.
My motion deals with the terms and conditions being imposed on the news media by Miss Inger Hansen in respect of their reporting of the inquiry which Miss Hansen is currently holding into an incident last November at the Millhaven penitentiary and the fact that this House should demand an explanation of what appears on the surface to be a very dangerous practice.

That the Standing Committee on Justice and Legal Affairs inquire into the restrictions placed on the news media by Miss Inger Hansen in regard to the inquiry into certain events at Millhaven penitentiary and report to the House whether this interference with the right of the news media to report freely and fully upon a public inquiry is justified in the circumstances.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I, too, have a motion under Standing Order 43. A task force report of the trilateral commission on ocean management warns of the danger of nations deciding not to wait for the end of the global treaty-making process and resorting instead to arrangements amongst themselves, thereby destroying the intent of the conference.
Since Canada has been negotiating and signing agreements with several nations on fisheries management, contrary to the advice of the commission, and since continuing pessimism is being expressed by an increasing number of countries as to the achievement of an international agreement on a 200-mile economic zone, many of those countries taking unilateral action, I move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That the Secretary of State for External Affairs make a statement on motions forthwith expressing Canada's position at the Law of the Sea conference in March, particularly to relate its plan if, indeed, as is obvious to the government itself, no international agreement will be reached.

speechtext:
am informed by the Departments of the Environment, Industry, Trade and Commerce and Finance as follows: 1. Using data supplied by the Soviet Union to the Internation Commission for the Northwest Atlantic Fisheries (ICNAF) on catches made within the Commission area, Canadian scientists estimate that Soviet catches within 200 miles of Canada's coast have been: 1970, 510,000 metric tons; 1971, 559,000 metric tons; 1972, 580,000 metric tons; 1973, 853,000 metric tons; 1974, 745,000 metric tons; 1975 to end of May, 227,000 metric tons.
2.	Canada intends to control foreign fishing within the 200 mile limit along the Canadian coast, but not to prevent all such fishing. At the Law of the Sea Conference, Canada is endeavouring to negotiate an international accord which will give Canada responsibility for the management and conservation of the fish stocks of a 200 mile "economic zone," and which will allow Canadian fishermen to fish to

January 26, 1976

their maximum capacity within conservation limits set by Canada. Foreign fishing vessels would then be allowed to fish, under terms and conditions established by the Canadian Government, within the zone for stocks surplus to Canada's needs.
3.	Soviet vessels are not permitted to fish within Canada's territorial seas and fishing zones, except for a small area of the territorial sea off the west coast, under the terms of a bilateral treaty whereby the U.S.S.R. have agreed to abstain from fishing in an area of the high seas of special importance to Canadian fishermen. On the Atlantic coast, "phasing out" and reciprocal agreements permit six other nations to fish in parts of the Gulf of St. Lawrence and parts of the outer nine miles of the territorial sea, under strict limits regarding the effort that may be employed. Beyond the territorial sea and fishing zones, the Canadian Government, at present, has no authority to control the activities of foreign fishing fleets, however, within the framework of ICNAF, quotas and other conservation measures are negotiated annually to provide for conservation of the stocks. Canada is not satisfied with the measures taken by ICNAF or with the adherence by some nations to agreed regulations. At a special meeting of ICNAF held in Montreal in September, Canada was successful in obtaining a 40 per cent reduction in foreign fishing effort for groundfish off the Canadian coast, and in having the Total Allowable catches for certain depleted stocks reduced to quantities that will allow rebuilding to higher sustainable levels.
4 and 5. The Soviet Union pays for Canadian exports in internationally accepted means of payment (fully convertible currencies) with prices determined by individual buyers and sellers at internationally competitive levels. None of our other trading partners are asked to make payment in gold and we have no reason to single out the USSR and prevent them from using the normal commercial means of payments. In any event, now that the price of gold is allowed to fluctuate according to international supply and demand it is not necessarily a more riskless form of payment than convertible currencies.

The plans for the additions to the Bank of Canada building on Wellington Street in Ottawa were approved by the Bank's Board in January 1972. The additions were designed to preserve the existing building and to permit the consolidation in one complex of all the Ottawa operations of the Bank, including those now housed in the Bank's King Edward Avenue building and in a number of temporary locations. The first and major phase of the work is now nearly ready for occupancy. When completed the additions will consist of below-grade space (three floors in most parts) for the entire area bounded by Wellington, Bank, Sparks and Kent Streets except for that part already occupied by the basement of the existing building, two twelve-storey towers flanking the existing building, and a garden court and bridges connecting the three buildings. The additional area will include 30,000 square feet gross of prime vault space, 246,000 square feet gross of other space below grade (to be occupied in due course by up to 300 persons engaged for the most part in high-security work),
13,000	square feet of garden court, 5,000 square feet of connecting bridges, 436,000 square feet gross of other enclosed space on and above grade, and some 60,000 square feet of open space on grade level. The additions will con

tain about 11.2 million cubic feet. The total cost of constructing the additions (exclusive of site purchase, architectural costs, landscaping, and interior partitions, furniture and furnishings and special-purpose built-in equipment) is currently estimated to be $45 million. Of this amount $29.5 million has been contracted for at fixed price contracts as a result of tenders, with a further $14.9 million contracted for on the basis of a guaranteed upset price with 75 percent of any savings being for the benefit of the Bank. The current estimate of $45 million compares with the estimate of $36 million released by the Board of the Bank in October 1971, the difference being due to the extent of about one-half to subsequent additions to the work planned and one-half to higher costs than originally anticipated. The land and buildings surrounded by Wellington, Bank, Sparks and Kent Streets were purchased by the Bank of Canada in ten transactions from 1936 to 1964. The area involved is 114,550 square feet. In the case of each individual purchase the price was negotiated following independent professional appraisal. The existing head-office building of the Bank, which was built in 1937/38, is being preserved but it will require some exterior changes and extensive interior renovation and modification to integrate it with the new buildings. The cost of architectural services, including structural, mechanical and electrical designs, for the additions is estimated to be $2.7 million. The architects are the associated firms of Marani, Rounth-waite & Dick, and Erickson & Associates, and they engaged and paid the consulting firms of C.D. Carruthers & Wallace, Ardec Consulting Engineers, and Brais, Frigon, Hanley & Assoc. Ltd. for structural, mechanical and electrical design services. The cost of services of other outside consultants involved in the construction and inspections of the building is estimated to be $400,000; this amount includes the services of van der Meulen & Associates, landscape architects. The prime contractors to date have been V.K. Mason Construction Ltd. for excavation work and Ellis-Don Ltd. for the construction. The contract with Mason Construction Ltd. was let in December 1971, and with Ellis-Don Ltd. for work on the sub-structure in June 1972 and for work on the superstructure in May 1973 and in December 1975. Landscaping costs for the Bank's own project are estimated to be $685,000. The Bank is in addition sharing with the Department of Public Works and the City of Ottawa the cost of developing the Sparks Street Mall between Bank Street and Kent Street. The interior partitions, furniture and furnishings, and special-purpose built-in equipment for the additions, including six pollution-free incinerators for burning soiled and worn bank notes, cancelled coupons and cancelled bonds, and a highly specialized system for vault and building security, are estimated to cost $6 million. speakeroldname: Hon. Mitchell Sharp (President of the Privy Council):
speakerposition: President of the Privy Council; Leader of the Government in the House of Commons; Liberal Party House Leader
subsubtopic: DEFENCE EXPORT SALES
speechtext:
I am informed by the Departments of Industry, Trade and Commerce, Supply and Services and External Affairs as follows: 1. (a) $12.25 (1974) (Canadian population taken as 22.9M). (b) Defence export sales by Canada in 1974 amounted to 280.5M. This figure was compiled on a contract basis (prime and sub-contracts) and includes applied research and development, pre-production, production, licence agreements and technical assistance, installation (other than construction) and repair, overhaul and modification. "Off-the-shelf" general procurement, construction, fuels and lubricants, basic raw materials, and services (such as rentals and transportation) have been excluded. Defence equipment sold by Canada has for the most part been items having a high technological content and includes such items as aircraft, aircraft engines and spares, airframe and engine components and spares, flight simulators, reconnaissance drones and spares, navigation and communication equipment and spares, avionics, marine valves, sonar equipment, ammunition and components, and vehicle parts and spares.
2.	The precise ranking of the value of military equipment sales by any country varies depending on the source of statistics used to arrive at the ranking. There are considerable variations in statistics emanating from different sources depending on the definitions and methods of compilation used, and uniformity and reliability is difficult to assess. The ranking of countries also changes from year to year. The four acknowledged world leaders in defence export sales are US, USSR, France and Britain. Several orders of magnitude below these countries is a group of countries consisting of Canada, Sweden, Italy, Czechoslovakia and China (PRC) whose estimated annual defence export sales over the last 10 years would rank them somewhere in the range of fifth to ninth depending on the year concerned.
3.	The Canadian Commercial Corporation has not been delegated responsibility by the Government to negotiate the sale of arms to overseas governments. However, from time to time, the Corporation does receive requests for such requirements from foreign governments and their agencies all of which are subject to the export control regulations of the Department of External Affairs and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce. It is to be noted that any such sales are strictly on a government-to-government basis and that the Corporation does not deal with any private firms or overseas commercial trading organizations.
4.	At present, there is no resolution before the United Nations for an international agency to monitor the sale of arms. In 1965-66 Denmark, Iceland, Malta and Norway sponsored a draft resolution to ascertain the position of governments concerning a proposal to register trade in arms with the Secretary-General. Canada supported this resolution but it was defeated, primarily at the instigation of many developing countries. This proposal was revived by Denmark in 1968 but the opposition was such that it was withdrawn prior to a vote. In 1968, the Honourable Mitchell Sharp, in his statement to the Twenty-third U.N. General Assembly, drew attention to the suffering caused by traffic in conventional arms. In 1971, the Secretary-General of the U.N. commissioned a report on the "Economic and Social Consequences of the Arms Race and of

Military Expenditures", which report was subsequently presented to the Twenty-sixth Session of the General Assembly as Document A/C.1/L.593. It was passed and was subsequently incorporated in Resolution 2831 (XXVI) which in summary was a resolution to keep a watching brief on specified consequences of the arms race. To date, unfortunately, all efforts to give substantive monitoring support to this resolution, through an arms register under U.N. auspices, have been opposed by a majority of member states.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
subsubtopic: AIRCRAFT "NEAR MISSES"
speechtext: The expression "near miss" has no official meaning in Air Traffic Services lexicon. Some states have attempted to define a "near miss" as a loss of separation between aircraft where the separation was reduced to less than 1,000 feet. However, in Transport Canada we speak of "Air Traffic Services irregularities", or "losses of separation" and they fall into two categories: critical and technical. The critical case could involve a loss of separation where one or both pilots in command took avoiding action, or there was no time to take such action, but the pilots concerned would have instinctively taken such action had there been time. A technical case is one where a loss of separation was reported but no avoiding action was considered necessary by pilots or controllers, but a report was filed. All losses of separation are investigated by a fact-finding board consisting of controller operations analysts from another unit and aviation safety officers. Findings and recommendations are made directly to the Director, Air Traffic Services, and the Director General, Civil Aeronautics whose offices ensure that appropriate corrective action is taken. The following critical losses of separation occurred in airspace controlled by Canada Air Traffic Controllers since January 1, 1974: (a) March 20, 1974. (b) Edmonton Industrial Airport, (c) CF-FUS, PA28 and Timeair 37/DHC6. (a) October 8, 1974. (b) 25 miles northwest of Moncton, (c) KLM flight 644, B747 and Capital International Airways flight 4902C, DC8. (a) November 3, 1974. (b) Vancouver International Airport, (c) Pacific Western flight 415, B737 and Air Canada flight 283, DC9. (a) June 11, 1975. (b) Toronto International Airport, (c) CF-VPK, Aztec and Eastern Airlines flight 308, B727. (a) August 6, 1975. (d) Following each such incident, the circumstances were thoroughly investigated by an Air Traffic Services Fact Finding Board, and appropriate recommendations were actioned, designed to prevent reoccurrence.

1.	Is James Skakie, a Canadian citizen, in jail in Mexico and, if so (a) when was he arrested (b) how long did he remain in jail before sentence?
2.	In December 1974, was his family informed that he would be released upon payment of $4,800 and, if so, was this sum deposited with the Canadian Embassy in Mexico City?
3.	Did the Canadian Ambassador advise his family that he would be released in October, 1975?
4.	Has he been released?
5.	Has his family been informed that unless they pay an additional $2,500 he will be held for another year?
6.	Will the Minister of External Affairs make appropriate representations for the immediate release of Mr. Skakie without further payments?

speakeroldname: Miss Monique Begin (Parliamentary Secretary to Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speechtext:
1. James Skakie, a Canadian citizen, was arrested in Mexico on October 14,
1973.	In September, 1974, he was sentenced. Under Mexican law, the courts have up to one year from the date of arrest to pronounce sentence, during which time an investigation and trial take place. It is normal for a trial to last from three to ten months.
2.	In September, 1974, Mr. Skakie was approached by a private Mexican citizen calling himself Mayor Pena who offered to effect his release for a payment of $4,800. Mr. Skakie informed his family by telephone of this offer. He was strongly advised by the Canadian Embassy not to turn over any money to anyone promising fast release by obviously extra-legal means. Mr. Skakie's lawyer was at this time appealing his sentence through normal legal channels. No sum of $4,800 was ever deposited by the family with the Canadian Embassy.
3.	In a letter dated May 15, 1975, to Mr. Morton Shulman, who was enquiring on behalf of the Skakie family, the Canadian Ambassador stated that the Mexican judicial system allows a detainee to be released on grounds of good behaviour after he has served two-thirds of his sentence; accordingly, Mr. Skakie would be eligible for release in October, 1975. It should be noted that release after serving two-thirds of a sentence is not automatic.
4.	Mr. Skakie has not been released. He has applied for release on good behaviour and the Mexican authorities are at present considering his application. The Embassy was informed by the Mexican authorities that, owing to a considerable backlog of cases, a decision on reduction of Mr. Skakie's sentence would be delayed.
5.	On September 5, 1975, the Embassy was informed by Mr. Skakie's lawyer that an appeal to a higher court had been successful and a bail of $2,500 had been set. If Mr. Skakie agreed to pay this bail, he would be relased from prison and deported, the bail becoming, in effect, a fine. This is a legal concession sometimes granted to foreign prisoners. This information was passed on to the family by the Department of External Affairs. Mr. Skakie was confident, however, that his application for reduction of sentence would be successful and that he would soon be released. He therefore decided not to post the bail. When Mr. Skakie was last contacted by an officer of the Embassy, he was still confident that his application would be successful.
6.	The Department of External Affairs and the Canadian Embassy in Mexico have been following this case very closely, and have frequently made representations to the Mexican authorities to ensure that Mr. Skakie obtain his full rights under Mexican law. As Mr. Skakie has been legally tried and sentenced, and as there is no evidence of discrimination against Mr. Skakie, there are no grounds for making representations requesting his immediate release. The Embassy will, however, continue to follow the case and assist Mr. Skakie to effect his release by normal judicial means.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this bill required little discussion at the second reading stage on Friday, December 12. It was dealt with expeditiously in the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs, to which it was referred and in which it was discussed on Tuesday, December 16. Likewise, I believe it will be dealt with in a few minutes this afternoon.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL ACT AND TO AUTHORIZE CONTINUATION OF PENSIONS PAID BY COMMISSION
speechtext: Don't be too sure, Stanley.

subsubtopic: MEASURE TO REPEAL ACT AND TO AUTHORIZE CONTINUATION OF PENSIONS PAID BY COMMISSION
speechtext:
There is one point which I raised at the second reading stage on December 12 which was dealt with in committee and concerning which I want the position to be very clear. This bill relates to the payment of pensions to persons who are still living as survivors of the Halifax explosion of 1917. Originally, some 1,600 or 1,700 persons were killed in that explosion and some 10,000 were injured. Over the years a good deal of money has been paid out in pensions, but according to the last report, the number still alive and drawing pensions is now down to 65.
When we debated this bill at second reading I expressed concern as to whether the Canadian Pension Commission, which will administer these pensions, from now on, would be a body authorized merely to pay out the pensions in amounts already determined or whether that commission would have authority to escalate pensions in accordance with the rise in the cost of living. I wanted to know whether it would have authority to deal with any new applications on the part of survivors, if there should be such new applications. During my speech on Friday, December 12, 1975, I asked these questions, as noted on

page 9985 of Hansard. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Trudel) rather disturbed me with what he said. He noted that I had asked my question, that there had been similar questions put by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), and then he said, as noted on page 9986:
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre was particularly concerned about that point

He was referring to the point concerning pension payments being escalated because of the rise in the cost of living. He went on to say:
-although the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants would also like to see the matter of pensions reviewed. I am wondering if this bill would permit such a review, or the inclusion of new people who are still suffering and are seeking some consideration. From my reading of the bill I am not aware of such possibilities. However, this point can best be raised in committee.
I am more or less satisfied with what was said in committee a few days later, and I shall quote the evidence given before the committee in a moment. But I feel that the questions I raised in this House should not rest with the negative statement made by the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance. As I said, the committee dealt with this matter on Tuesday, December 16. The hon. member for Halifax-East Hants referred to the questions which both he and I had asked. He was answered by Mr. Allan O. Solomon, chairman of the Canadian Pension Commission, the body which will administer these pensions in the future. Mr. Solomon said, as reported on page 79:14 of the Minutes of Proceedings and Evidence of the Standing Committee on Finance, Trade and Economic Affairs:
Mr. Chairman, we have-or we will have-from the Halifax Relief Commission the formulas which they have been using, and which they established some years ago. I would anticipate that we would use those formulas as a starter and from there, depending again on how much money there is available for the purpose, we would eventually try to evolve a formula which we feel would be fair to all concerned, and try to relate as much as possible to the disability pensions which we pay for similar types of cases on the war disabled.
Then the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants asked this supplementary question:
Would the pensioners, Mr. Chairman, be then on a similar footing as say somebody who had suffered severe injury in the trenches in the first world war?
Mr. Solomon replied:
They are not on a similar footing financially now, and it is hard to say of course in advance if they would become on a similar footing later. But certainly we would hope to bring them as close together as we possibly can.
The answer given by the chairman of the Canadian Pension Commission is reassuring, and the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance said more or less the same thing, but in different words, when the matter was before the committee. The issue, as we all know, is important. There are now not more than 65 persons drawing these pensions. Some of us are in touch with some of these persons. On December 12 I mentioned a boy, four years old, who was blinded in the Halifax explosion of 1917 and who has been blind for 58 or more years. He is now approximately 62 years old. This man's pension has been increased a bit during the years, but has not kept pace with the rise in the cost of living; nor has it kept pace with what has happened to war disability pensions.
January 26, 1976

I think we all agree that those who suffered from the Halifax explosion of 1917 were, in effect, in the front line of World War I and that they should be treated that way. I know that veterans' organizations in this country feel that way, and Mr. Solomon and the other members of the Canadian Pension Commission feel that way as well.
I am not asking that there be an announcement in the House that these pensions will increase by a certain percentage, or what have you. However, I would like the matter to be clear. Since the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance is here and has not yet spoken at the third reading stage, he can speak now and I hope he will make it clear that under this legislation the Canadian Pension Commission has the authority that Mr. Solomon said to the committee he believes the commission has.
As I pointed out when I spoke on December 12, I do not think it is good enough for us to make the Canadian Pension Commission a bookkeeping agency that merely carries on what has been decided, because it is a dynamic situation; there are these 65 people still alive and there could be situations in which survivors with dependants might be making new applications for pensions. I want the Canadian Pension Commission to have the same authority to consider new applications and to review the levels of pensions arising from the Halifax explosion that it has with respect to war disability pensions generally.
I am sure I speak for all who are interested in this matter, interested because some come from that area or interested because some of us actually remember at least the news of that terrible explosion in 1917. We applaud the decision to find some other means than now exist for carrying on this work. We think the decision to have the Canadian Pension Commission handle the matter is wise and we support it. We also approve of the provision in the legislation that says that when the job is all done, when there are no more survivors and no more pensions to be paid out, any money left over is to go back to Halifax for further rehabilitative work in areas of Halifax that were affected by the explosion.
I do not want to suggest that I am older than members of this House think I am, but for those of us who remember that catastrophic event it is interesting to know that this work of humanitarian mercy has gone on over these many years. We are glad to know that it will be carried on as long as it is necessary. However, we hope the word will get out to those who are survivors that if they have a case for a higher level of pension than they are now receiving, the Canadian Pension Commission will have authority to deal with their claims.
I am sure all of us in the House are ready to support this bill and give it third reading. However, I hope that the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Finance will in fact welcome the opportunity I am giving him to correct the statement he made on second reading, and make clear that under the legislation the Canadian Pension Commission will have the authority that Mr. Solomon seemed to think it would have once Bill C-78 has been passed.
Halifax Relief Commission

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think I join the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles) who voiced some concern about the answer I gave in the month of December last at the time he was asking questions. I did say that those questions could certainly be answered in committee. As he indicated himself, Mr. Solomon who appeared before the committee at that time answered as the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said he did. At that time, the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave) was asking the same questions, and I think that he too had the same concerns. He was concerned, hoping that people who had really suffered and who were suffering or who had an aggravation of the injuries they had sustained at the time of the explosion or after could turn to the Halifax Relief Commission and ask for a revision of their case to get some increase in their pensions.
I think Mr. Solomon answered very well, and quite clearly. Contrary perhaps to the doubts I had expressed in this House he voiced an opinion that was clear and specific, and that must be noted, as the hon. member did.
As to the distribution of the amounts of money that could remain after all the pensions will be paid out, there is clear agreement, the legislation is quite clear about that. There is no doubt that the funds will be well used to improve the city of Halifax or the surroundings where the explosion took place.
The hon. member also pointed out something about the new distribution of the funds. I think that happened in the past, and we were always interested in relieving the people who were referred to us. However, I do not think I left the impression that there had been changes in that respect. I think that Mr. Solomon was quite clear, that his interpretation is still the same, that the people of the Canadian Pension Commission are becoming administrators, that there had been no change of policy in the government position but only new administrators. I agree with the interpretation the hon. member kindly gave of the remarks made by Mr. Solomon, and I think that all members want at least relief for those who suffer, even if the number is restricted. I think that the sufferings of those people are much greater than what one imagines, and I ask for the sympathy of all members of this House.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to emphasize two or three points to supplement what was said at second reading stage by the hon. member for Halifax-East Hants (Mr. McCleave), what was said in committee, and what was said in the House this afternoon by the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). In my judgment, the Pension Commission should interpret clause 2(3) generously. That is the clause the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre has been discussing. I assume it gives the Pension Commission power to pay pensions to applicants for the first time and to adjust the level of existing pensions.
A great deal of time has gone by since the catastrophe in 1917. With the passage of time, cost of living increases and other factors, it is imperative that those responsible for administering these pensions review their level urgently

January 26, 1976
Halifax Relief Commission
and frequently. In addition, the Pension Commission must be prepared to receive sympathetically new applications and, indeed, applications which the Halifax Relief Commission may have turned down, because nobody is beyond mistake. I cannot emphasize too strongly the importance of the Pension Commission approaching with an open mind applications which may come before it. It must not approach an application on the basis that it had been dealt with already by the Halifax Relief Commission on some day gone by.
In the interests of those who suffered from the explosion, or believe they did, it is important that they not only be dealt with fairly but believe they are being dealt with fairly. It is my hope that the Pension Commission will review the level of existing pensions urgently and frequently and will approach new applications with an open mind, including any that may have been rejected earlier by the Halifax Relief Commission.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre said he would be pleased to suggest ways of disposing of any money which might be left over after the needs of pensioners, or potential pensioners, had been looked after. I wish to emphasize that the aim should be not to have anything left over, and I am sure the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre would agree with me. The aim should be to see that the money which was set aside for the purpose is used in its entirety to help those who suffered in the Halifax explosion. I hope the Pension Commission will not worry about having money left over, in terms of helping the part of the city which was damaged, desirable though that might be. I repeat, without apology, that the Pension Commission should approach its task on the basis that the money should be made available to those who suffered as a result of that catastrophe in 1917.
I should like to emphasize, too, that the Pension Commission should take special measures to ensure that there is adequate liaison in the Halifax area to serve the needs of the pensioners and those who may for one reason or another feel it desirable to make application to the commission under the bill before us. It is important that these men and women receive adequate service and that there be satisfactory liaison arrangements on the spot. Indeed, I would go so far as to say that the Pension Commission should associate with itself, in the discharge of these responsibilities, some well informed person from the Halifax area, not for the purpose of continuing to ensure that the commission continue to apply the same principles and follow the same practice as the Halifax Relief Commission-this might not be desirable in every case-but, rather, for the purpose of making certain that the commission and those dealing with applications are fully familiar with the local circumstances affecting cases.
I shall not keep the House any longer. I am prepared to have the bill passed on third reading on the basis that the commission will be fully authorized to increase existing pensions or to grant new pensions where it sees fit. As I resume my seat, I mention again the importance of the Pension Commission adopting the attitude that this money is for the benefit of those injured in the explosion of 1917, and I hope the commission will not worry about trying to

leave money over for some other purpose, desirable though that other purpose might be.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I wish to participate in this third reading debate following some of my colleagues, notably the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil), who also made a proposal, and the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton) who made another proposal. This proposal was put forward by the members of our party in the hope that the government might, even at this point, reconsider its position. If they must go through with the bill in its present form, unacceptable though it is, they might within a year draft amendments or, if necessary, redraft the bill in such a way as to meet the requirements of those for whom it is intended. At the same time, it could be presented in such a way as to be understandable to the producers themselves.
The legislation before us embodies many shortcomings. Some of these were pointed out in the course of previous debates. I have just mentioned one of them: nobody understands it. It provides for payments to producers despite the fact that they might not need payments in a particular year. In fact, payments might be a disadvantage to them because they might find themselves in a higher income tax bracket. Conversely, payments are not made in years when they are really needed. Payments to those who qualify are made a year late, and that is not when they need the money; they need the money during times of depressed prices, low sales, or while the effects of natural hazards are being felt.
To remedy a few of these shortcomings, I should like to put before the House what I consider to be a proposal which should be considered. It would meet many of the objections I have noted with regard both to this bill and to the previous bill, the original Bill C-71, which was stillborn. The bill before us looks as though it might be born, but it will require immediate surgery; it will require blood transfusions and it will certainly require a lot of attention. The proposal I am about to put forward is one which I believe should be carefully considered and one which will be placed before my constituents and all others who care to participate in a discussion of this nature. I hope it will be picked up by other members of our agricultural caucus and perhaps amended or changed to suit local requirements, and thereafter will become part of a Conservative plank in our agricultural platform in years to come.

January 26, 1976
What I am proposing is a cash assurance program. Everything seems to have a short form nowadays, and if hon. members wish, they can simplify that title by calling it CAP. I think this proposal will, in time, perhaps eliminate the need for several programs now in existence. For example, my proposal would incorporate the cash advance and crop insurance programs. The scheme could be expanded so that not only grain but cattle sales and sales of other agricultural products could be included, whether in western Canada or any other part of Canada. Although initially we included only grain sales in the three prairie provinces, my proposal could be worked out in such a way as to include other areas of Canada once the rough spots have been ironed out.
My proposal would also provide an annuity for those who may not qualify for any payment. This would overcome another objection. Any producer participating in the scheme whose income exceeded the maximum would, under the proposal of the minister, not qualify for any payment. My proposal would be this: rather than the 2 per cent suggested by the minister, the annual contribution by any producer initially would be 3 per cent at least; it could be even more. Since the government is willing to pay $2 for every $1 paid by the producer, I would adopt this principle so that the government pays double the producers' amount into the fund. Indeed, contributions could be increased. Taking into account the fact that at the present time the government is proposing a 2 per cent levy on all grain sales, and that any producer with crop insurance coverage pays a premium of 4 per cent to 5 per cent of his total grain receipts, this really amounts to 7 per cent in premium.
My suggestion would be that the producer should pay 3 per cent. Since the government contributes 6 per cent, this would mean a combined premium of 9 per cent of total grain sales. At the present time, crop insurance premiums are approximately 10 per cent of total coverage. Since the government pays half the premium, this means the producer is paying roughly 5 per cent. Thus, producers would have no hesitation in paying up to 5 per cent, or whatever percentage was required, so long as they received money when they required it, that they did not receive payments when their incomes were high, and that each individual producer was considered, on merit or amount of production, and they would have an annuity if not receiving other benefits.
A look at the table of rates of premium for crop insurance discloses that the premiums, as a percentage of total coverage, drop as the number of farmers participating increases. Starting from about 1971, the premiums were roughly 15 per cent of total coverage. They went down to 13 per cent, stayed there for a little while and then dropped to 12. For 1975-76, they are down to about 10 per cent of total coverage. This represents an involvement of 93,000 farmers from 46,000 in 1971.
My proposal would be universal, because every farmer would have to contribute. At the present time, some would back away from this because there is a maximum and they would have nothing to show for their contributions when they retire. All they are being asked to do is to put money into the fund, which is a bottomless well, but my proposal takes into account producers who might reap no benefit
Grain Stabilization
over their years of operation. I have set, arbitrarily, the maximum amount of assurance at $30,000. This could be adjusted and is a matter for further consideration, but for the sake of my argument this afternoon I have set it at $30,000. If production increases, this maximum could be increased to $35,000 or $40,000.
The averaging rate would be the average income of the previous five years. As soon as a producer has taken off his harvest, he can proceed in the same way as under the cash advance legislation, go to the fund and withdraw the whole of his five-year average, or 90 per cent of it or 80 per cent. The only restriction I impose is that the withdrawal should be in denominations of 10, to make the calculation easier. The advance could be repaid at the same rate as the percentage taken out. In other words, assuming a producer's five-year average was $10,000, if he withdrew only $5,000 the repayment on any sale he makes would be at the rate of 50 per cent. If he withdrew only $2,000, his repayment rate would be 20 per cent of total crop sales. If he made a $200 sale of grain, 20 per cent of the amount would be deducted, plus the 3 per cent premium or whatever rate was established as repayment for that particular year.
This proposal would provide farmers, or producers, with the necessary cash, which is why I call it a cash assurance program. A farmer who knows his production for a particular year, and therefore his cash requirements-which can be calculated very readily-can go to the fund at a time when he needs money, rather than wait a year before his receipts can be calculated, and then perhaps receive a payment the following year when he may have a bumper crop or sales have boomed. Under my proposal for cash assurance, the producers could have cash when they required it.
During periods of low income there would be a forgiveness provision. This would be calculated the following year, since one would not know one's total receipts for the year beforehand. The amount of forgiveness would be at the rate of 9 per cent. We have the 3 per cent that the farmer contributes during the year if his cash receipts are low, and we have the 6 per cent that the government is prepared to contribute, and this is the two for one basis that the government is proposing. In other words, if a farmer's five-year average was $10,000, the forgiveness for that year would be at the rate of 9 per cent, or $900. If sales were $9,100 for that particular year, there would be a $900 payment made to him. If, for example, his sales were $9,800 and his five-year average was $10,000, his forgiveness for that one year would only be $200. In other words, this would not be a flat, across the board payment, but would depend upon the amount of the sales in the particular year.
Let me give another example. If the five-year average was $10,000, and the producer's sales were only $5,000, the amount required to bring his income up to the five-year average would be another $5,000, so his forgiveness would be $900. Therefore, the amount that would be carried forward would be in the form of a loan in the amount of $4,100.
This fund would be a loan scheme and an assistance scheme at the same time. It would also include annuity features to the benefit of those farmers making contribu-

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
tions but not benefitting. For example, the $4,100 would be carried forward following the end of the crop year, with a further six-month period of grace within which it could be repaid. If the amount had not been fully repaid, then interest charges would be added at the rate of perhaps 10 per cent, or perhaps the rate of interest for the average bond or the rate at which the government is borrowing its money.
All we will be doing is setting up a fund from which the farmers, the producers, can get money when they need it. In this way, they would not be taking out money each year and investing it in some other area, perhaps making more money in that way, while the government is searching out other sources of money supply. The producers would have a responsibility under this fund. They would have to pay a penalty of perhaps 10 per cent in respect of any unpaid advances. If, at the end of the year, a producer had quit farming or had retired without repaying the entire amount of the advances, an additional penalty or charge of 1.5 per cent per month could be added. In other words, there would be this inducement to the producer to make payments into the fund. This would be particularly true if a producer left farming and was no longer making sales from which advances could be taken, because there would be this penalty or charge of 1.5 per cent per month on the unpaid balance. These charges could be made until the entire amount of the advance had been repaid.
The scheme would also contain a provision for complete repayment in one lump sum. For example, if a producer had $4,100 lying around, not being used, he could pay off the entire advance without having the repayment related directly to 20 per cent or 50 per cent of his sales. Let us assume there are some people who have incomes which average over $30,000, or whatever the amount might be per year. They would not be eligible for advance payments or loans from this fund. After a five-year period during which a producer had not received an advance or a loan, it would become obvious that he was not a burden on the fund: he would be making contributions all the time, and in this event his contributions would automatically be reduced.
Perhaps after five years without an advance being made to the producer, his premium rate could drop to 15 per cent or perhaps 12 per cent. The producer would continue to pay the premium, but this adjustment or refund could be made by way of a cheque. After five years, or perhaps eight years, the premium rate could drop from 15 per cent to perhaps 12 per cent, and so on. In other words, the premium rate would continue to go down. I think all crop insurance schemes have a premium reduction feature built into them, and perhaps the people who operate those schemes could be of assistance to us in this regard. We could take advantage of their knowledge and experience as to the best way of repaying these benefits to the contributor. Obviously there will be some producers who will not draw benefits or take advantage of the scheme because their annual income is better than the five-year average. Perhaps they will just prefer not to take the cash assurance payment. There will be some people whose income will be lower than the average but they will manage to get by without the advances. These producers should be granted something similar to a bond status. Since the plan would be universal, all producers would be making conti-butions. This could be extended to apply to all farm sales,

including grain, potatoes, cattle, fruits and other agricultural produce.
It goes without saying that all producer sales must be recorded in a production book, including farm to farm sales. It would be absolutely essential to have a complete accounting. Since there would be many who would not take advantage of the benefits, there would be a build-up of funds. Many of these people might feel they were getting nothing for the contributions they were making to the fund. These people, under this scheme, would be making contributions on which interest would be paid. This would be an advantage to those who left the money in. Upon retirement, or perhaps after ten years of contribution, these people would be able to withdraw their equity in the fund. This would obviously be an incentive even to those who had never taken advantage of the scheme.
In the initial stages, everyone would be asked to make contributions in order to build up the fund. I am sure every farmer would be prepared to make such contributions in order to assist his fellow farmer, knowing full well that there may come a time when he will need assistance. This is just like the situation with crop insurance; a farmer may insure for year after year and never be required to draw on the plan. Perhaps he drops his crop insurance, and the next year experiences a crop failure. I am sure producers would have no hesitation in making contributions to such a scheme. This would be particularly true if they knew their funds were increasing in value through the payment of interest. They would have the advantage of being able to withdraw their equity after a period of time, increased by the amount of interest paid perhaps based on the average government bond rate.
I suggest my plan takes into account the complaints we often hear from people who say they derive no benefit from such schemes. In summary, let me recite some of the advantages of this scheme. We could eliminate the need for crop insurance and have participation by everyone. There has always been hesitancy on the part of some to participate in crop insurance plans. I am sure there would not be the same hesitancy on the part of producers to contribute to this type of plan.
Second, there would be universal participation, which could eliminate the need for crop insurance and for cash advances because cash advances and the crop insurance idea would be incorporated. Third, the plan could be expanded to include grains, cattle and other products, and all farmers in Canada. Fourth, it would provide at least an average income to each farmer every year: in other words, there would be stability of income. It would be for the producer to determine whether or not to participate if his average was below the five-year average; the onus would be on him. This would eliminate, at a time when disaster strikes, the need for petitions to be submitted to the government and the government finding itself in the awkward position of treating these people as if they were an underprivileged group asking for a hand-out.
Fifth, there would be an incentive to produce and carry on good farming economics, because as sales increase even over the five-year average, so does the average income increase. There would be an incentive for the farmer to
January 26, 1976

produce over and above his five-year average and not wait for a forgiveness, because if his sales are over the five-year average, his next year's average and eligibility would increase. Sixth, no premiums would be collected during low-income periods. I am suggesting that there be this forgiveness amount which I have already calculated. At a time when money is needed, the producer should not be asked to pay premiums. The difference is that under the proposal of the government, at a time when there is most need, an additional half per cent is added. That is an absolutely backward step.
Seventh-and this is a very important point-each producer would know precisely how to calculate his five-year average using total sales during this period, including farm to farm sales. Even to this date, despite all the studies carried out; most members of the House still are unable to figure out the formula. All that would need to be done under this proposal would be to tabulate the total sales over the past five years and work out the average. This would make it possible for people to learn what they might expect. Eighth, if no assurance payment is taken, premiums would be reduced. In other words, there would be an incentive not to take any money, because the premiums would be lower. Ninth, it does not pay producers to increase revenue during periods of high income and then have to repay the money in the form of income tax, at higher income tax rates. Producers would have a forgiveness provision and assured income during depressed periods, all economic factors considered.
What will happen under the government's proposal is that if the producers have a bad year, according to the way the minister has figured it out now, the calculation will be made a year later, and if in the meantime they make large sales and received payments, all the money will go back to the government in the form of income tax at higher rates. In my proposal there is an attempt to avoid this. Tenth, to those who do not benefit directly, this proposal assures a return on equity while the producers would be involved in a plan which would help others in need in the industry.
In other words, under the proposal I am putting forward if, for one reason or another, because of regulations, the fact that they do not wish to participate or because their sales continually increase because of good management, good luck or what have you, they do not need to take any funds out, then they should be paid not only their equity because it was used to finance others, but should be paid at the bond rate or at some other figure that would be reasonably close to the bond rate for that period.
I have set forward what I believe is a proposal which takes into account the majority of the objections heard by members of the committee when they travelled to western Canada. I think the plan is considerably simplified. It eliminates the need for two other different schemes. It takes into account the objections of those who felt there was no advantage to them. I think that this proposal, if it is not acceptable to the government at this time, should be placed on the record for the benefit of those who may wish to consider it. There may be those who would wish to amend it. Unlike the minister, I would be only too glad to receive suggestions concerning improvements.
I believe I have covered the majority of the objections which have been presented to date. I believe there is a need
Grain Stabilization
for some sort of cash assurance program, but I certainly do not believe it should be the type of proposal the minister has put forward. The proposal of the minister is confusing and at times would place the farmer in a dilemma. It will not meet the requirements of the western producer. I hope my proposal will be given consideration. I hope that in the months to come the farm groups will consider it, and prior to the next election we may put it forward in a polished and refined form if the minister does not accept these changes now.

subtopic: MEASURE RESPECTING THE STABILIZATION OF NET
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to take a few moments of the time of the House to register the reason I cannot support this bill. The bill might have been of some value had it been oriented differently and had got to the nub of the problem, which is how to stabilize the individual farmer's income at a time when he needs it. This stabilization bill does not recognize that the western grain industry is made up of some 200,000 farmers or managers. It treats them as if they were one incorporated whole.
This bill would waste a great deal of money that could be used in a better way. This type of bill would be more suitable if the industry were dominated by two or three large corporations or production units, as is the case in respect of the automobile industry. However, this is not the case. The agricultural industry is made of many individual units. I think this is the weakest part of the bill. It will not meet the needs of the producers for a very long time and certainly will be subject to change.
Furthermore, taking in the six main grains and oilseeds upon which the pay-out is based and the premiums deducted really assumes that all farmers in the grain growing areas of the prairies have the same farming practices. Of course, this is not so. There are very large farms, but with a great deal of difference in productivity one from the other, this diversification, in the long run, makes for a very good agricultural industry, which is much better than any of the monolithic structures such as those of the U.S.S.R. The bill does not recognize the great difference between the individual farmers concerned.
As one who comes from a parkland area, I must say that the mechanics of the pay-out will tend to discriminate against those who farm and live in the parkland areas of the various provinces. The reason for this is quite obvious. The production of wheat there is not as great, compared with the production of coarse grains, barley, oats and oilseeds, as it is in southern Saskatchewan, parts of southern Manitoba, and Alberta. Yet the condition which will trigger the pay-out will largely be set by the situation with regard to wheat, because wheat accounts for something like 70 per cent of the total grains income covered by this bill. Because the plan makes no allowance for the fact that while wheat is the dominant grain involved, individual producers of oilseeds and coarse grains, particularly in the parkland areas, could find their incomes reduced, but if the wheat income remained high, there would be no pay-out whatsoever.
This stabilization bill is an attempt to correlate and consolidate the many different plans which have been introduced in the last 25 or 30 years to provide a measure

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
of stabilization to the grain industry. For instance, PFAA dates back to 1939 or 1940. I think, on the whole, that program was reasonably successful for its time, and I still think that elements of PFAA should have remained on the legislative books, because I found it was especially effective in helping very small producers. While many of these small producers may, in a sense, be social problems, they are very necessary in adding to the sum total of farming; but they are not likely to take advantage of this program. PFAA did help the very small producer who never got around to buying crop insurance and who was not a good enough manager to take care of things as well as he should. He found that PFAA was very useful to him.
Acreage payments were quite effective in many ways. They did not come automatically every year; therefore, they did not have built into them the system which the stabilization bill will have-an increase in the saleability of land. In other words, the capital cost will eventually reflect the amount of money paid out under this plan. The assistance on storage of grain which costs, relatively, a lot of money and which it was alleged made the grain handling companies storers of grain rather than sellers, contributed a good deal of money which presumably assisted farmers. It cost the federal treasury a fair amount of money. Presumably, some or most of it eventually benefited farmers because it at least took the grain off their hands; and as most grain handling companies belonged to the farmers, most farmers should have benefited in the long run.
This grain stabilization program will not be a very effective method of providing much money where it is needed. According to some research on the effect this bill would have had on the plan had it been in effect over the last 20 years, it would have given to the farm industry an average of some $50 million per year, whereas under various programs, various governments have already paid out an average of over $70 million per year. So grain stabilization, which is supposed to improve all the earlier plans, will in fact contribute less money than was paid out under them.
Of course, the dollar value in years to come will be greater, but that will only be because of the inflation factor. In addition, this $50 million payment assumes that everyone is in the plan. There are many things wrong with the plan and a large number of producers will not find it in their interests to participate in it. Quite likely it will be much less than the equivalent of the $50 million which I mentioned. It is more likely that about one-half to two-thirds of that amount will be paid out. Unless and until a stabilization plan is introduced which will deal with the problems of individual producers and will allow them to draw on the program when they need to, that is, when their economic conditions are such as to warrant pay-outs, it will be of no great value. In the future perhaps this plan could be expanded for the individual producer in some manner; only then will it become a useful tool to aid producers in distress.
During the early 1950s, when atomic bombs were being made, we heard a great deal from the Americans about more bang for the buck, which meant they wanted to make atomic bombs in the cheapest way possible. This type of program will mean a lot of bucks for a small bang, because it does not single out the needs of the individual producer

and separate him from the mass. For those producers who want to opt out, the government is obviously not making it very easy. I am told they will have to write to the Canada Grains Commission in Winnipeg. At a meeting in Regina a week or two ago, that is what an official from the minister's department said. However, there will be no soliciting and no reminding individuals that if they wish to opt out, they have the right, and they will not be told who they should contact. This is typical of the sleight of hand of government departments and some governments.
Each producer will have to make up his own mind whether he should stay in the plan. Frankly, for the older producer who may be retiring in another ten years or so, there does not seem to be much advantage in staying in the plan. There is no provision for recovery of premiums at death, or retirement from farming, although I believe there would be a benefit for two years after ceasing farming, or a producer could sell. However, it will be a very nebulous thing to sell his land because of the relatively small amount of value it will carry. If there were a better provision for recovery of premiums at death or upon retirement, this bill might be more acceptable. In particular, I wish to direct the attention of the House to the fact that producers must make their own decisions.
The minister has failed, in this legislation, to provide a reasonable solution to the problem, because he has insisted that a global plan is the only plan which can be introduced, when in fact it must be related to the needs of the individual farmer before it will reach its greatest value to the grain industry. We have crop insurance which is based on the individual. Why not introduce a plan that would allow the individual farmer to capitalize on the program and use it to best advantage when he needs it, rather than give him a large amount of money? That might often fall in the best year he ever had, and then he would have to give it back to the government through income tax. I would predict that this plan, tied to the global plan as opposed to the individual plan, will return, through income tax, a large portion of the money paid out. I think we must consider, first of all, what is best for the individual and what it will take to bring him through a tough economic period.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the bill before us for third reading is one that we have dealt with in this House, off and on, for the past six years. As a new member in 1968, it was one of the first pieces of legislation that I dealt with, and I believe in 1969 or 1970 we had first reading of the old stabilization bill. We all know the history of that bill, Mr. Speaker. It was opposed by every farm organization, wheat pool, the Federation of Agriculture and the Farmers' Union, as well as by this party and the Conservative party. As a result, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board was forced to withdraw it. Now we have the daughter of that bill, in different form. I think this one is better than the old bill because it recognizes a few of the deficiencies in the old bill, but still there are some things which need to be improved, and in this third reading debate I want to point out a couple of them.
For years this party has said that in this country we need a universal farm stabilization bill to cover all commodities. For years, too, the farmer has faced the problem
January 26, 1976

of fluctuating income. He never knows what he will receive for his crop when he plants in the spring, or what he will receive for a hog when it matures. I think it is our responsibility, as parliamentarians, along with provincial legislators, to devise a scheme whereby the ups and downs in the market pattern are smoothed out for the producer, so that he will know at the beginning of the year what income he is likely to receive. From growing up on a farm, and through my experience in representing a rural riding, I know the farmer would produce a lot more food than he is at present if he could be assured of the price he would receive.
Mr. Speaker, I was shocked by a comment made by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) today, to the effect that there is too much dairy production in this country, too much skimmed milk, and that the world cannot use any more. If we have the capacity to produce, it should be an objective of the Department of External Affairs and our foreign aid programs to encourage farmers to produce as much food as possible can, to help feed the hungry of the world as well as a lot of people in this country. A few months ago a report on poor children pointed out that many in this country are not receiving adequate nutrition.
When we talk about the stabilization of farm income in this country, we should also talk about a food policy. I am very concerned that in 10 or 15 years, unless we start a national plan to maximize production, build storage capacity and a delivery system, we may face a shortage of food in this country. The Minister of Agriculture has said that he does not like to see eggs go rotten, or a surplus of powdered milk, but we could not deliver them to Bangladesh or other countries which need them. That is a sad commentary on a society that can produce tons and tons of surplus food but cannot deliver it to areas of the world where people are dying of malnutrition, and cannot even deliver it to the children of this country who are suffering from malnutrition because there is not adequate milk or food in the school system.
We talk about stabilization of farm income in this country and say it is a worthy objective, but the only way we will get it is through a program that will guarantee the farmer a stable price for his produce. There are many examples of farmers who would like to produce hogs, for example, or to expand or diversify, but they dare not because prices are depressed or because of the uncertainty of the market. They cannot afford to make a huge initial capital investment under these circumstances. Your Honour is aware of many of these problems, coming, as you do, from a riding in the centre of the huge farm belt in southwestern Ontario.
As parliamentarians, we should be able to provide farmers with the same security as other people in this country. The worker has the trade unions to bargain for him, he has unemployment insurance plans, and so on. The business community has all kinds of guarantees. The Conservative party gets upset when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) makes a revelation that any idiot knows is true, that the free market no longer exists. We all know that there are many kinds of support for the business community. There ought to be adequate support for the farm population as well. This party has spoken of farm income stabilization, marketing boards, maximizing production, more adequate
Grain Stabilization
world aid programs, food banks, and so on. I believe this bill takes only a small step in that direction. There are many principles that should be incorporated in an adequate farm income stabilization program.
Since this Minister of Agriculture took office there has been no sign of a long-term agricultural policy for the country. There have been only ad hoc measures. There has been no concerted effort, and no indication of the direction the minister intends to take us. We get bits and pieces of various programs, but no long-term program. When the bill was introduced, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board called it a significant step. In a paper issued by his office in September, 1974, he said he had four general objectives for the plan. I should like to go over them and point out some of the deficiencies in the bill.
The minister said that he wanted to protect grain producers in designated areas from uncertainty and variation of return due to temporary market fluctuations. Such an objective is honourable. The minister is talking about this plan as an income insurance plan. He is going to average cash flow for farmers for any particular year over the previous five years. It is an honourable objective, but I am afraid the plan does not live up to it. The way payments are made out of the plan can affect a lot of farmers in this country. The plan is based on aggregate income. This means that if the aggregate income applying to growers of the six grades of grain falls below the previous five-year average, there will be a pay-out to all participants in the plan. That sounds good. But what is to happen to rapeseed growers if the bottom falls out of the rapeseed market? I suggest that if the bottom of the rapeseed market falls out, even though the price of wheat may go up, or the price of the other five commodities remains stable or goes up, the rapeseed producer will not receive a pay-out even though his income may decline drastically. That will be the effect of applying the average. You take into account the price of all grains. Wheat is the dominant grain, and the price of wheat may go up or down. But the rapeseed market may decline and the rapeseed grower will not get a pay-out from the plan. That is unfair.
The plan lacks flexibility. Farmers in Yorkton-Melville whose income declines because they have produced a lower grade of wheat, or because the market price for their wheat has gone down, will not get compensation if the average price for the other grains remains high. Of course, the converse is also true. Suppose world rapeseed prices are buoyant but wheat prices are coming down. If the average price, taken over the previous five years, of all grains produced under the plan falls below the five-year average, there will be a pay-out not just to wheat producers but to producers of other commodities including producers of rapeseed. That shows the type of logic behind the plan.
Let me draw an analogy which may help to explain some of the serious questions concerning this plan. Let us suppose unemployment insurance worked the same way. We would look at the total income of all working people of this country and, after taking into account increases in the cost of living and other factors such as the inflation rate, if it were found that the income of workers in Canada had fallen below that of the previous five-year average, the unemployment insurance fund would make payments. It
10312

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
would not make it just to the unemployed, but to all Canadian workers, including high school teachers, clerks, factory workers, and so on. The payment would be made to all, no matter if they were employed or unemployed. It would be made even to members of parliament if they were to pay unemployment insurance, which they do not. But the point is this: all those who had contributed to the plan would receive a payment from the plan. Payment would be based on the amount paid in.
Another section of the bill says that' payments from the stabilization plan are to be proportionate to the amount you contribute. As I say, if this were true for unemployment insurance, the worker who had been unemployed for a good part of the year would receive little help, because his contributions were small, whereas the man who had been employed all year would receive a large pay-out from the fund. Clearly, this bill is inconsistent with other stabilization plans enacted in this country.
What would happen if the medicare scheme were applied on the same basis? Take the man who needs expensive, open-heart surgery and runs up huge medical bills. At the end of the year he would only be partially compensated by the plan because his payments in had been low, whereas, say the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) who goes into hospital for treatment of a hanging toenail-

speechtext:
-or ten hanging toenails, as the hon. member says, he can get his condition corrected and the payment out under the plan would more than cover it, while it would not nearly cover open-heart surgery. That is the type of plan being foisted on the farmers of the prairie region. Or, suppose automobile insurance was applied that way. I have not had an accident for a long time, fortunately, but let us say I receive compensation and there is a pay-out from the automobile insurance plan in Saskatchewan. I get it from somebody, say. But the driver who may have written off his car, been involved in court cases and had to compensate somebody else for bodily injury, would receive only a small pittance as a pay-out from the automobile insurance plan of Saskatchewan, if that plan worked as this plan will. That is the philosophy behind this plan.
As I said previously, the bottom may fall out of the rapeseed market and the income of rapeseed growers of my riding may fall. But at the same time the price of the other grains mentioned in the bill may stay high. Because the plan considers the aggregate price of all six grains, rape-seed producers will not get a pay-out even though they have suffered. That is not fair. What would happen if we operated medicare, unemployment insurance, automobile insurance and the educational system in accordance with the philosophy contained in this bill?
Incomes across the prairies fluctuate. Your are talking not just about one province; you are talking about Manitoba, Saskatchewan, Alberta and the Peace River country of British Columbia. You will see many fluctuations in types of crops and soil and the application of various cost factors. In one part of the prairies you may see bumper crops and in another part poor crops. The people of southwestern Saskatchewan may enjoy bumper crops and high prices, but there could be a crop failure in some other area and the

bottom may fall out of the price for the grains grown there. It would happen, under this plan, that not only those losing money would get a pay-out; those raking it in would also get it. It is the plan's lack of flexibility to which I object.
I submit that with some additional cost-and perhaps a few administrative headaches-the plan could be made flexible. It could be one which all farmers would be happy to join. This would encourage farmers to produce food not only for this country but for all the people of the world. But this plan does not work that way. Under it, payments out will be based on the amount of money you have put in.
Some members of the Conservative party are worried about our Prime Minister's gallop toward socialism. My goodness, if this is the type of philosophy the government is putting forward, it is anything but progressive. It is not the philosophy under which we send our kids to school. It is not the amount of money you can afford to put into the school system which determines if your kids are to be sent to school. I have just returned from a visit to South America and learned that the money in your pocket dictates the quality of medical attention you receive. Really, that is the philosophy of this bill. It should not be. Pay-out should not be based on what the farmer has contributed to the plan. If a farmer is experiencing difficulty, he should receive a pay-out from the plan in the same way as an unemployed worker receives unemployment insurance. This plan ought to operate as other so-called universal plans in this country operate. A plan like that would be progressive and would help this country's farmers.
On September 4 the minister said that the second objective of the stabilization plan would be to ensure that growth and development of the grain sector was consistent with the basic market forces and that the grain sector developed in a manner consistent with competitive advantage in world open markets. There the minister was talking about open market forces. He was talking about things which are really not relevant to the need for food production today. He was talking about the laissez-faire system, the market system of the world-

speechtext: Which the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) says does not work.
