speechtext:
-which the Prime Minister, as the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) says is not working. It has not worked for a long time. Any who do not know this are either naive, or a much more descriptive adjective could be applied to them. This is a time when we should be talking about an international grains agreement, when the countries of the world should establish long-term agreements regarding world food banks, providing food aid and working out a food distribution system. Yet this government has sponsored many plans in this country which militate against that type of philosophy. I need only mention the two-price system for wheat. I do not think the minister has to be too worried about this being a plan that will be consistent with world open market forces.
The minister says, in the same paper, that the third objective is that the plan will be complementary to the development of the livestock industry. Again, I do not see the relevancy of this. If the parliamentary secretary
January 26, 1976

speaks, perhaps he could comment on this matter as well. We see in this country the failure of a lot of people who produce livestock. When times are good, they get together and have a marketing board for their commodity so that there can be more stable production of livestock in this country. The last objective he comments on is that the plan will be based on a set of principles consistent with general objectives for agriculture which could be applied to other commodity groups. As I have already stated, I do not see that general plan coming from across the way. I do not see the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, or the Minister of Agriculture coming up with a general set of objectives as to what Canadian agriculture should be involved in. What are their plans?
I have talked about some things I would like to see in the world in the eighties and nineties, the world before us, in terms of maximization of food production, a world delivery system and a world food bank. We in this country can produce food. We can work with countries that have money in order to produce food to better the human condition of us all. I would like to know the objectives of this government. How does this plan fit into the long-term objectives of the Canadian government?
Another concern about the plan is that it leaves out of the computation of the costs of production a number of items that are very important. I notice it leaves out the interest a farmer must pay on his machinery, equipment and buildings that are necessary for the production of grain. As anyone who has visited a grain farm knows, this is a major cost of producing grain. It leaves out the 2 per cent levy, the maximum of $500 the farmer will pay to help finance the plan we are dealing with today. It also leaves out depreciation on machinery, equipment and buildings. These are very important factors in producing a bushel of grain, cultivating an acre so that it is ready to produce grain.
I received in my office this morning confirmation of what we think is an important factor left out of the formulation we are dealing with today. I received from the minister of agriculture of my province a letter containing the latest statistics in Saskatchewan. It sets out how much it is expected to cost to produce a bushel of grain. I would like to spend a few minutes looking at the actual cost of producing a bushel of grain in Saskatchewan. These statistics were compiled by the department of agriculture in Saskatchewan. This is done on an annual basis from the sources they have, such as farm organizations, Statistics Canada and other reliable sources. This is the type of work we should be looking at.
According to the statistics, the average cost of producing grain on an acre of land in Saskatchewan, in 1975, will be $57.10. I want to deal with the specific components of that. It is important that it be put on the record. The cost summary per acre of grain is as follows. Cash costs and seed, and most of these items are specifically included in the cost of production, will be a factor in the bill. There are others I will deal with later that are not. The average cost of building repairs per acre of land is 45 cents. This includes the grain bins and the other buildings a farmer must maintain. With regard to machinery and equipment, fuel and oil costs $1.25 per acre. As everyone knows, the price of fuel in this country will escalate rather than go
Grain Stabilization
down in the years to come. Repairs, tools and hardware cost an average $3.65 per acre of grain.
As the hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre pointed out, we hear every week, especially in the spring and during harvest, about farmers having difficulty getting machinery repaired by dealers. Parts must be ordered from great distances. This adds to the farmer's cost of putting in a crop, having summer fallow or taking off the crop at the end of the year. Custom work hired averages 55 cents. Crop expenses, less seed, averages $3.85 per acre. This includes such things as sprays and other necessities. The cost of purchased seed is 90 cents per acre. Home grown seed is $2.50 per acre. Taxes, landlord costs and overheads average $2.95 per acre. When you total the cash costs and seed, you get $16.10 per grain acre.
We then go to depreciation. That is not a part of the formula in this bill for calculating production costs. In Saskatchewan, in 1975, depreciation of buildings, and improvements, was 80 cents per acre on an average farm. Depreciation on machinery and equipment is $6.30 per acre. This adds up to $7.10 depreciation per grain acre in Saskatchewan. I made a calculation. Depreciation on those items alone, which are legitimate production items, works out to 12 per cent of the total cost per grain acre. That 12 per cent is not included in the production costs as defined by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board.
I move to the next item that the farmer has to pay- interest. Interest on land, in 1975, was $14.40 per grain acre in Saskatchewan. It is legitimately argued that this should not be a part of the cost of production. I accept the argument made by the minister in charge of the Wheat Board, even though I know some people do not. Interest on buildings, and improvements, in 1975, is 70 cents per grain acre. That is a legitimate cost of production to be calculated under this act. Interest on machinery and equipment averages $3.80 per grain acre. That, too, is part of the legitimate cost of production. Total interest, therefore, on buildings, and improvements, machinery and equipment is $4.50 per grain acre. That is 8 per cent of the total cost of producing an acre of grain. That makes 20 per cent of the total cost per grain acre that is not included in the cost of production. It is a very relevant factor when calculating the pay-out to the producer if there is to be a pay-out from the plan. It is important in determining that a pay-out will be triggered. Hired labour averages 70 cents per grain acre, and unpaid family labour is 60 cents. An operator costs $13.70. The total labour cost is $15 per grain acre. The total cost to produce an acre of grain in Saskatchewan is $57.10, 20 per cent of which is not covered under this bill.
There is another factor that was not a factor in Saskatchewan in 1975. I refer to the 2 per cent levy that will be charged to producers when this bill comes into effect. Therefore, an additional 1 per cent or 2 per cent must be added to the cost per grain acre. This was not included in the cost of production figures. It can be safely said that 21, 22 or 23 per cent of the cost to the farmer for producing an acre of grain will not be included in the computation under the bill we are dealing with today. If the bill included some of these costs, it would be more acceptable to grain farmers in western Canada as well as to opposition members. I am sure that privately it would be more acceptable to many members on the government side. It would certainly expe-

dite passage of the legislation through the House of Commons so that it could become law in this country.
1 could go on at length talking about why depreciation of these items and interest on them should be calculated and should be part of this bill, but I think hon. members get the general idea from the comments I have made and the statistics I have read into the record. There are many other things which concern me and farmers in my area about the bill, but I am hopeful that the minister will take a serious look at the arguments which we in the opposition and members of farm organizations have put up and will not exhibit a stubborn streak when analysing the arguments we have made. Because we in the opposition, I assure you, Mr. Speaker, are speaking in the best interests of the farmers. We are not being political. We are not being partisan. We are being nice guys; we are doing our work and we are doing it hard: we are putting forward constructive criticisms.
The minister, with a nice smile, is acknowledging that we always do this. I want to say to the minister that I hope he will do that in a sincere way, because if he does not, this bill will fail and it will be another black mark upon the conscience of the government vis-a-vis the farmers. I have said for so long that the farmer is the greatest gambler in the world. He gambles on the weather; he gambles on world grain prices. But why in the devil should he gamble on the Liberal party? They can change that if they would, to a certain small degree, take into account the suggestions which we and the farm organizations have made. If this bill does not work as it should, they should not hesitate to come back and put down amendments. If they do not do that, the act will not work; and if they do not have the co-operation of the farmers, the legislation will not work.
The objective must be to stabilize farm income at an adequate return upon which a farmer and his family can live and enjoy all the good things in life that the average Canadian has had for a long time without worrying about his income. At the same time, we should encourage the farmer to produce more food so that the people of this country and the people of the world can be fed, and so the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. MacEachen) and the Minister of Industry, Trade and Commerce (Mr. Jamieson) and others are able to devise a plan whereby we can deliver that food, deliver the goodness we can produce in this country into the mouths, the bellies of those who need it, from one corner of this world to the other. If we do that, we as Canadians will have made one small contribution to the betterment of mankind.

The House resumed consideration of the motion of Mr. Lang that Bill C-41, respecting the stabilization of net proceeds from the production and sale of western grain and to amend certain statutes in consequence thereof, be read the third time and do pass.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in rising to speak on this bill for a few moments on behalf of the wheat growers I represent in central Alberta, I want the minister to recognize that they are not overenthusiastic about this bill. In fact, I think they are as unhappy as I am about this legislation because of the fact that the minister did have an opportunity and plenty of time in which to bring in legislation which would have been of benefit to the prairie grain producer. Perhaps this bill will go down in history as "the lost opportunity" of the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board (Mr. Lang). Surely the hon. gentleman has had enough association with the grain producers, along with his hon. friends from Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) and Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac), to have brought in legislation which could really have served a useful purpose.
I cannot understand why the minister is not prepared to listen to suggestions or to make changes which could be of benefit and serve the producers. After all, when this legislation is put in place, as I presume it will be with the support of the Liberal party, it is going to be very difficult to alter it in any way. While it is true the producers are vitally concerned about the effects of this legislation, we must also recognize that every taxpayer in Canada is interested in it, because for every dollar the producer pays, the taxpayers of Canada are putting up two dollars. I am sure that if it were not for this carrot the minister is dangling before the eyes of the grain producers, the bill would be entirely unacceptable to them.
At the present time, when producers are receiving a fair price for their investment, the minister in charge of the Wheat Board comes along and says, "We shall take away a portion of that money and put it away for you." In other words, he is acting just like a big daddy does toward his sons or daughters, saying, in other words "We do not trust you with your own money; we shall take care of it for you."
January 26, 1976

Let me assure hon. members that these people who have used their initiative and their ability to work long and hard hours, the people who have the resilience and the dedication to continue to produce crops in western Canada, have far more to offer than many of those who have been elected to the House of Commons.
I am very sorry at this time to be part of a system which is only doing a small percentage of that which is our responsibility. I feel this bill is only going a very small way toward doing what is required for the benefit of all the people of Canada, and especially the grain producers. It makes me sad when my constituents feel, because I have been elected to the House of Commons, that I am a member of the government rather than a member of the opposition, particularly when the minister will not listen to the proposals we make in an effort to make the legislation run smoothly for the benefit of everyone.
I have a comment here from a small paper in one of the finest wheat growing areas in Western Canada, Three Hills. It is as good as Saskatchewan; I do not say it is better, but it is just as good. Some of the farmers at this meeting wanted to know how the government's contribution to the program was to be raised. They also wanted to know what the chances were for a plebiscite. Other information sought included an explanation of the way in which costs of production would be calculated, and whether funds would be reimbursed when a farmer retired. These are questions which are of the utmost importance to these producers. If some type of explanation had been provided by the minister in answer to these questions, the program would have been far more acceptable. It is apparent from talking to farmers throughout the constituency that they are not greatly interested in this bill. If you want to talk about the subject, you have to raise it yourself. They are not concerned about it because they know that it is not going to do the job for them.
Had the minister communicated with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) to a greater extent and tied Bill C-41 with the crop insurance program, I am sure the producers would have taken a careful look at it. Let me impress upon you, Mr. Speaker, that the crop insurance commissions in western Canada are vitally concerned at this point in time about this bill and what it will do to their program. The Minister of Agriculture, both in the House and in committee, expressed with glee the fact that there was increasing participation on the part of the producers of western Canada. Now that the austerity program of the government has been implemented, it has been suggested that cutbacks will be made in the government's support of the crop insurance program. Thus, I believe the crop insurance commissions should be concerned that this will be a deterrent to the participation of producers in the crop insurance program. There may be hard times ahead for the crop insurance commissions and for those who rely on crop insurance, and this will not be in the best interests of western Canadian producers.
Another point that should be made is that if grain prices drop over a period of six, seven or eight years, the pay-out at the end will be very minimal. After an extended period of low grain prices there will be no help of any substantial nature for the producers. I should like to put on record
Grain Stabilization
what one farmer said at a meeting. He was critical about the five-year average basis for triggering payments and suggested that it would negate any substantial benefits from the program if grain markets were depressed for a long period. He also was concerned that the program might cause a degree of instability in that farmers might react by abandoning their own methods of income stabilization.
I can understand that, Mr. Speaker, in view of the complexity of this bill. Both the hon. member for Qu'Apelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton) and the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) expressed the fear of farmers in their areas that they might feel their incomes will be protected whereas in fact they will not. As both hon. members pointed out, if the scheme were operated on an individual basis, each producer would know exactly what he could expect from the program. At present, he has no way of knowing. If producers think they are being protected and they find out they are not, the situation for many producers of grain in western Canada will be chaotic.
This is why I feel the minister has short-changed the producers of this country. For example, certain regions of the country may not have had a crop for a number of successive years and the farmers' incomes may have dwindled due to circumstances beyond their control, say climatic conditions or other reasons. They would have received no income from their production. Under the present program no provision is made for such producers. They will not be provided with that which will keep them in business.
The problems of the western grain producers are becoming ever larger and more complex, and adequate programs of one form or another must be put in place for them. They should, on an individual basis, be able to put money away in the good years, tax free, and withdraw it during periods of low production, and at lower cost. There are so many ways that the program could have been made to work and be of benefit to the producers. Nevertheless, the minister is adamant: he is not going to change any provisions in the legislation. He has been very difficult to deal with all the way through passage of this bill, whether at second reading stage, in committee or at report stage. In fact, in committee he changed his position. He first said that crop insurance payments would not be included in the agreements, but had to reverse himself on advice from his departmental officials.
We are dealing not only with legislation that will not do the job it should, but with legislation that will supersede existing legislation and will hinder the enactment of legislation that could be put in place in years ahead. It makes one very sad to realize that the grain growers of western Canada are being shortchanged, which is what is happening at the present time.
I hope the hon. member for Assiniboia, when he rises to speak on this bill, as I presume he will, will try to prove why the government is unwilling to bring in a program that will support crop insurance. Had the Minister of Agriculture accepted our suggestions when he brought in the crop insurance bill, we would not need to pass this legislation today. It is because of this lack of imagination on the part of the Minister of Agriculture that we are dealing with this stabilization bill. I go on record, Mr. Speaker, as saying that it is also because of the lack of

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
imagination on the part of the minister in charge of the Wheat Board that we are dealing with this legislation down the road. There is no way the legislation can fulfil the purpose slated for it or be satisfactory to the grain producers. As a result, it will not get the support that is required to make legislation like this work.
Another of the shorfalls of the legislation is that it will mean a further increase in bureaucracy. This has been a sore point for me. Right from the start I felt that any program like this should be initiated and administered by the crop insurance commissions of the three prairie provinces and the Peace River bloc in British Columbia. There is absolutely no reason in the world why the program could not be administered by the headquarters of the three prairie administrations, instead of Ottawa. If this government had wanted to give a certain degree of authority to another part of Canada, this would have been a prime area to do so, as well as a wonderful opportunity for the three prairie crop insurance commissions. But no, the minister refuses to do this; apparently he wants the legislation to be under his thumb.
Perhaps the reason is, and I can think of no other, that the minister wants to build his own empire. There is absolutely no room in the political arena for any individual member of parliament, minister of the cabinet, or anybody else, to build an empire, because the minute you start doing that, the administrative efficiency deteriorates and the government does not then operate for the benefit of the people. We are here with the challenge to bring in good legislation which will be for the benefit of those we have to serve. I am sorry to say that is not the case in respect of this legislation. I want the people that I represent to know that I am unhappy with this bill because I know that at some time in the future we will have to deal with this matter again. There are too many inadequacies in this measure for it to serve any useful purpose.
As I pointed out to hon. members this afternoon, there are many people in their senior years in the agricultural industry who will never take advantage of this legislation because some time in the near future they intend to retire. Most of them will never participate in this bill, short of there being a disastrous drop in either production or the price in future years. Soon after they retire there is no longer any way in which they can benefit from the premiums they will have paid. For that reason alone I think this is bad legislation.
I am sorry this House has been unable to bring forward a better piece of legislation. That being the case, I should hope that in the not too distant future we will deal with this matter again, as I am sure we will, because the producers will demand that the inequities in this bill either be reconciled or corrected with future legislation.

speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I think the list to which you have referred is one where time ran out before everyone on it had been given the opportunity to take part in the debate before the recess. At that time my name did not come forward and I did not have the opportunity to speak during the debate. I thank you for recognizing me at this time.
I must say, as I begin this afternoon, that I have been interested to hear the comments by members of the official opposition party as well as those by members of the NDP regarding the legislation before us. To a certain extent I regret, not the substantive comments they have had to make about some of the problems they see in the future in respect of grain farm income, but the pessimistic and rather gloomy tenor and tone of what they had to say. I do not share that pessimism. I believe very sincerely that this particular moment is an historic one, historic for this parliament and for the government of Canada because of the nature of the bill we are dealing with now and, most importantly, it is historic for the grain producers and the economy of western Canada. We are now nearing what I hope will be final approval in the House of Commons and, hopefully, soon approval in the other place as well, for Bill C-41 respecting the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I say "hopefully" with some optimism, as I sense in the House this afternoon a willingness to give this measure third reading in a fairly short period of time.
Recently, grain producers in western Canada have gone again on record in a very clear and categorical way with
January 26, 1976

their wishes in this respect. I think it is important to take account of this. Farmers have, once again, made it abundantly clear in the past few weeks that they support this legislation, that they want it and want it as soon as possible. I hope this expression of opinion will carry some weight with all hon. members of this House. I should first like to refer to a press report which appeared in the Thursday, December 19, edition of the Regina Leader-Post under the headline, "Pool Supports Bill". I should like to quote part of that report, for the information of hon. members, as it appears in the Regina Leader-Post as follows:
The board of directors of Saskatchewan Wheat Pool has called on all members of parliament to facilitate passage of the federal government's grains stabilization bill. The pool directors are concerned that provisions of the plan be passed into law as soon as possible.
The directors stated that ample time and opportunity has been provided for all interested parties wishing to suggest amendments to the stabilization bill. "Saskatchewan Wheat Pool notes that the House of Commons standing committee on agriculture held a series of hearings throughout the prairie region this past summer in which opinions of farm people were heard and proposed amendments discussed.
In addition, various farm organizations and individuals have advanced their views on the subject in briefs and other representations," the directors said.
The article goes on at some length. That is a very important expression of opinion which I hope will find some favour in the House as we consider this measure. I would also like to quote from a newspaper article that appeared recently in the Manitoba Co-Operator under the date January 15, 1976. This is a very important farm newspaper published in the province of Manitoba. Under the headline, "Farm Bureau Urges Income Stabilization", the article reads:
The representatives of the bureau also endorsed a resolution which called for a recommendation to go to the federal government that the western grains income stabilization bill, known as Bill C-41, be adopted at an early date and certainly prior to the completion of the current session of parliament. The bill is in its third reading at the present time. The meeting directed that letters urging the passage of this legislation be sent to Mr. Lang, agriculture minister Eugene Whelan, and the leaders of the opposition parties and all members of parliament from Manitoba.
Finally, I should like to put on record sentiments expressed recently at a very important annual meeting of farm organizations in western Canada. I am referring to the Western Agricultural Conference which involves members of the Unifarm from Alberta, members of the Saskatchewan Federation of Agriculture, the Manitoba Farm Bureau and United Grain Growers. As a result of their annual meeting held recently in the west, this organization at this conference forwarded a message to the minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board which reads as follows:
Western Agricultural Conference members meeting in Regina January 15 adopted the following policy:
"That the grains stabilization legislation be adopted at an early date and certainly prior to the completion of the current session of parliament."
As I say, that message was from Alberta Unifarm, the Saskatchewan Federation of Agriculture, the Manitoba Farm Bureau and United Grain Growers. I must say I found that expression of opinion from a very broad crosssection of the grains industry in western Canada to be persuasive, and I hope other members of this House will
Grain Stabilization
find the same kind of import in those words from these various groups in the west. These words are really a repetition of the full support for Bill C-41 which came through very clearly in our committee work on the legislation. I think, for example, of the very detailed, thoughtful and thorough brief presented to us by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture when our Standing Committee on Agriculture met in Edmonton on June 16, 1975. The CFA put forward a careful and reasoned analysis of this bill. They discussed several specific recommendations for changes, many of which, I hasten to point out, we have been able to accommodate already in the amending processes which have gone on prior to this moment. On this important matter of farmers' support for Bill C-41, I wish to refer hon. members to the manner in which the Canadian Federation of Agriculture began its important presentation to the standing committee. It began with this paragraph, and once again I think it is important to put these words on the record:
The Canadian Federation of Agriculture supports the passage of this legislation. The federation believes it is decidedly in the interest of the prairie grain industry and the prairie and Canadian economy to have a stabilization plan of this nature.
That is how the CFA began its presentation. I think it is important to note the words the CFA used in concluding that presentation to the Standing committee. Once again I am quoting from the brief presented to us on June 16 in Edmonton:
Finally, but very importantly, we recommend the plan enter into force for the year 1975. Our members have made their wishes on this very clear, emphasizing the value they place on this legislation.
Unfortunately, we have already passed the deadline of 1975, but certainly the purport of their recommendation is that this is a good bill which should be approved by the House at as early a date as possible. I find that an important expression of opinion, coming as it does from one of Canada's most broadly based representative and producer-oriented organizations. This obvious producer-based support for Bill C-41 was a consistent theme throughout our committee work. As brief after brief came forward from farm organizations, there were a number of suggestions for changes or amendments to the legislation, but the context in which those recommendations were put forward was always the same: it was a context of support for the bill.
As I say, many suggestions for strengthening the bill were presented by many groups. Many of these ideas have already been incorporated in the amendments. It might be useful, in a summary way, to review what some of those amendments have been. For example, we have expanded the voluntary nature of the plan to ensure that new producers who begin operations some time down the road may also have full opportunity to exercise their option, if they so choose, using their own good judgment about their farm operations; to be out of the plan if that is their judgment. The voluntary nature of the plan has been expanded.
We have removed the previous limits on the participation of multiple-unit farms. We have referred the matter of interest rates and the maximum level of gross receipts to the producer advisory group that is set up under the legislation. We have undertaken conscientiously to examine the matter of regionalization about which we have

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
heard today and earlier in our discussions of this legislation.
At the report stage, in addition to a series of amendments proposed by the minister designed to simplify somewhat the mathematics involved in the bill, we accepted amendments which made specific our desire to include in the plan about 90 per cent of eligible grain sale proceeds and to require a full report to parliament at the end of the first three-year period of operation. These have been major amendments despite the comments we have heard from some in this House who would suggest that they are rather minor. They are amendments which were largely suggested to us by farm organizations which presented representations to us in our committee hearings.
We have dealt with them in response largely to these producer representations. They represent, I suggest, a sensitive responsiveness to the proposals made by the farmers and farm groups, individuals and groups which, as I said earlier, have repeatedly come forward to make suggestions for improvement, always in the context of supporting this bill and seeking to make the bill better. That much good work indeed has been done.
I should like to address a few remarks in relation to some of the comments we heard today, and on the occasion before Christmas when we had a chance to discuss this legislation at third reading stage, about the matter of individualizing the plan or the question of regionalization. First, I wish to deal with the matter of individualization. We have heard what amounted to two widely different approaches to this particular question, one expressed by members of the New Democratic Party and the other expressed by members of the Conservative party.
They are expressed in similar terms in that they each use the word "individualization", but I think members of those two parties would readily agree that the approaches they are suggesting are radically different. First of all, the NDP approach, which as I assessed it received some support from the spokesman for the National Farmers Union who appeared before us, and by some provincial governments in western Canada, notably Saskatchewan and Manitoba, in principle amounts not to a grain income stabilization program or a commodity stabilization plan in any way, but really to what is more properly described as a guaranteed income scheme which has, as I view the situation, three rather undesirable attachments to it. First of all, it would be my expectation that the NDP proposal for individualization would serve to eliminate what are real and legitimate differences between good and bad farming judgment and good and bad farming practices. I do not think one would find very many farmers in western Canada who would want those legitimate differences between one farmer and the next eliminated by a government plan.
Second, the NDP proposal could possibly, and I would suggest quite likely, distort or provide artificial insulation against real and inescapable production and marketing signals which producers should be able to see and hear. I think hon. members opposite would agree that was one of the most important concerns voiced by the Palliser Wheat Growers Association when that association presented its brief to us at our hearings in Regina. They did not want the plan to be artificial or distorted, or to get us away from the real world in which we live.

Finally, one of the objections I think farmers generally would have to the proposal for individualization put forward by the NDP is that it seems to me that kind of a concept inevitably would lead to greater interference in, and control over, the individual producer's operating decisions. That would be an undesirable result, and I think an almost inevitable result of the proposal they are making. I think it is an unwanted result. It certainly is unwanted from the perspective of grain producers.
Now I should like to turn to the proposal put forward by the members of the Conservative party. As I begin, I want to thank them for the conscientious way in which they have approached this question. I refer particularly to the proposal of my hon. friend from Moose Jaw who I think has done a great deal of work on this idea. Unfortunately, I cannot agree with his proposal, for reasons which I hope he will agree are substantive and reasonable.
First of all, having taken a serious look at his particular idea and the mathematics of it, and having gone through some calculations based upon what he had to say, it is my judgment that the proposal he has made would serve to reduce the level of federal contributions and commitments to the stabilization program. It would reduce the level of over-all protection for the grains industry and individual producers. Indeed, it would make the plan less effective in total. That can be seen only by going through the full set of calculations and working out what his proposal would amount to, or what his party's proposal would amount to, compared to the proposal of the government.
The mathematical calculations are rather long and detailed, but when you come to the final line and compare the value of the government's plan, on the one hand, with the value of the alternate proposal on the other, the figures are very clear. In the long run, the net protection for the grains industry or for individual producers would be substantially less under the proposal put forward by my hon. friend from Moose Jaw on behalf of the Conservative party. So, clearly, this business of individualization is not an unmixed blessing. It may be simpler to explain if you can put it in those terms, but it does not lead simply to a better plan for western farmers.
On the matter of regionalization, as opposed to individualization, I think I can deal with that matter very simply once again by referring to a specific recommendation on this point made to the government and to parliament by the Canadian Federation of Agriculture when that organization appeared before us. On page 3 of their brief they recommend that we provide for intensive study of the regionalization option and the legislation for its adoption if this should prove desirable.
They were not suggesting that we march forward immediately with regionalization, but that we look at it seriously, recognizing that it too may not be an unmixed blessing, and that we study the question very carefully before going forward with it. It may well have some merits, and hon. members have discussed those potential merits in the House on many occasions, but CFA suggested that we look at it carefully, analyse the pros and cons, see if it can be feasibly and reasonably done, and then, if that proves to be the case, that some time later down the road
January 26, 1976

we go ahead with it. That is a reasonable recommendation, and indeed before the standing committee the minister made it clear that that kind of examination of the question would be undertaken.
We have heard a great deal in this House today and on previous occasions about the cost of the administration which will be involved in handling the western grain stabilization plan. This could be of some concern because we have heard a great deal about thousands of bureaucrats descending upon the west, interviewing farmers, causing them a great deal of extra fuss and bother, and about extra costs mounting to hundreds of thousands of dollars every year going down the drain in the administration of this plan. Those have been the stories and the rumours, and they may be entertaining, or in some circles politically popular, but they are simply not factual; they are not true. In the first year or two of the program naturally some extra expenses will be involved in the start up process, and some extra costs may be incurred in the survey work which will have to be done at the outset, but once the plan is in place and functioning it will be interesting to look at the facts and to see what the presently projected administrative figures turn out to be in reality.
The estimate at the present moment is that the permanent administration of the western grain stabilization plan will involve some 12 to 15 people. It is planned that they will be located in a rather small office of the western grain stabilization administration located in the Canadian Grain Commission building in Winnipeg. A total cost of something in the range of $300,000 per year on an ongoing basis is likely to be required for the administration of that office and of the plan.
Some argue, as we heard earlier today in the discussion by the hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Towers), that the crop insurance programs would be a more desirable mechanism for the administration of a plan of this kind. It has been suggested that that would be a cheaper and more effective way to administer an income stability program. If the matter were that simple I think we might be inclined to follow the suggestion of my hon. friend and of crop insurance boards elsewhere in the country, but the facts simply do not support the case.
It is interesting to consider some of the specific figures. I refer to the figures for 1975-76 and the cost of administering crop insurance programs in the three prairie provinces. The important figure to consider is the projected administrative cost per insured farmer for the year 1975-76. First, for the province of Alberta it is estimated that the administration costs will work out to be something very close for $80 per insured farmer. For the province of Manitoba it is estimated that the administration costs per insured farmer for 1975-76 will work out to something in excess of $80 per insured farmer. In Saskatchewan the comparable figure is something in the range of $65 per insured farmer.
When we consider the administration of the western grain stabilization plan and include all the feasible costs which could be involved, and based upon certain assumptions about participation levels in the plan, it works out that the projected cost per insured farmer under the western grain stabilization plan is something in the range of $11 or $12 per insured farmer. That is $11 or $12 compared with $65 for crop insurance in Saskatchewan and with
Grain Stabilization
approximately $80 for crop insurance in Manitoba and Alberta.
Those figures are pretty important, and I think they show that the administration of this plan is likely to be substantially less costly than the crop insurance programs now in place. It is interesting to note as well that all administrative charges for the western grain stabilization plan are not borne by the fund established under the legislation, but rather by the general treasury or the general revenues of Canada, by the taxpaying population of the entire country. It will not be borne by the specific goal oriented contributions made by government and by individual producers to the stabilization fund.
Finally I wish to deal with a matter which has been raised in the course of this debate, and I think it is important. It has to do with the complexity and detail involved in this legislation. It has been suggested that it is too long, detailed, and complicated. To begin with, what we are dealing with is a long, detailed, and complicated problem. It is a problem which goes back to the very beginnings of western Canada. We are all familiar with that cyclical pattern of grain incomes-up one year and down the next-which shakes the western grain industry to its very boots.
Our problem is not a simple one. It is a fundamental challenge which has faced the grain industry and successive governments of various political stripes in this country over the years. It is not a simple problem to solve in just a few words or with a simple plan. It is a complicated problem requiring a detailed and, I suggest, complex approach.
It has been suggested that the earlier bill which came forward some four or five years ago was simpler than this one. This suggestion refers to the old bill, C-244, but I hope hon. members will also remember in comparing that bill with this bill that the older bill was a compulsory plan. Producers and other people suggested that this plan should be voluntary. We have made it essentially voluntary, but by doing that we have necessarily added some complexity to the legislation.
It had been argued that Bill C-244 of four or five years ago was defective because it was on a gross basis and not on a net cash basis. That argument was accepted by the government, and the bill has been improved. It is a stronger bill because it now takes into consideration the cost of production. It is based on the net cash position of farmers, and because it is improved in that respect it has also necessarily become more complex. Good features which improve legislation also, unfortunately, add to its complexity. That is a fact which is inescapable.
Also important is that despite the defect which some hon. members see, and despite the fact that the legislation is complex, there is also a very important advantage in that because everything affecting the calculations is in the bill. It is all spelled out in detail for farmers, parliamentarians, and everyone in the country to see. Nobody can change those calculations. Nobody can change the rules without coming back to parliament to do so. I have heard hon. members opposite complain rather bitterly about the fact that government tends to do so many things by regulation and by orders in council. Well, this is one measure where

that is not so because everything affecting the calculations is specifically spelled out in the law itself.
I do not deny that this bill is complex. I quite agree with hon. members that it is a long and detailed bill. However, if it is complex I suggest to hon. members on all sides of the House that that necessarily places an important burden on each one of us, not necessarily to go out and sell the bill if we are not inclined to do that, but at least to go out and explain it factually and rationally to producers in our respective constituencies across western Canada so that they, at least, can have the facts and the basic information before them, and so that they then can make a rational judgment for themselves about the grain stabilization plan. We on the government side ask hon. members to carry out that responsibility. We do not ask them to go out and promote the bill if that is not deemed to be in their political interest, but at least to go out and explain the facts rationally and fairly so that producers will have a full and fair opportunity to exercise their judgment under the legislation.
Hon. members might ask how is that to be done, how we suggest they explain the legislation. I think it could be done in a number of ways, and just for the information of the House I should like to tick off a few of those which hon. members might find interesting.
This is one of the ways in which that particular effort of explanation and information was carried out in the constituency of Assiniboia. Hon. members will recall that the bill was introduced on December 4, 1974. Ten or 12 meetings were then conducted across the Assiniboia constituency. Farmers and the public were invited to discuss the legislation in its initial form in January, 1975. Then there was a province-wide open line radio program on CBC where the same general discussion was invited on the bill as presented to parliament in its original form. Following that, across the length and breadth of Assiniboia and other constituencies, because media patterns happen to overlap, there were at least seven detailed articles in weekly newspapers telling in a fair and unbiased way what the stabilization plan was all about.
Then there was a series of news releases and press reports advertising the hearings of the Standing Committee on Agriculture to be conducted across Canada. I have heard hon. members complain that nobody knew about these hearings, that they were secret and that farmers were not given a chance to appear. But those hearings were advertised in all the weekly newspapers in Assiniboia constituency. I did a head count on one occasion, and most of the people in attendance at our hearing in Regina, in the middle of the hearing week in western Canada, were from Assiniboia.
Advertisements were placed in the weekly newspapers and paid for by the member of parliament telling of the specific calculations that would be made available to individual farmers who wanted to know what the plan would mean to them. That information was given publicly to members of parliament by the minister when he appeared before the standing committee. He extended a blanket invitation to anyone who wanted to know what the plan would mean to them. All they had to do was send

in their gross grain receipt figures to an address in Regina and the information would be provided to them. That was advertised across the southern part of Saskatchewan, which I have the honour to represent.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in the early part of October, 1975, there were 12 more meetings in four days. Once again farmers were invited to attend and hear about the bill, to make comments and ask questions before final consideration in this House. Full details of the legislation were provided, a slide show was offered and leaflets were available for farmers to take home and study. There was also a question and answer period. Every corner of the constituency of Assiniboia was covered. It might be useful to mention the places involved-Avonlea, Mossbank, Gravel-bourg, Glentworth, Rockglen, Assiniboia, Bengough, Rad-ville, Milestone, Torquay, Sedley, and Weyburn.
After that there was final open line show in November on the largest privately owned radio station in Saskatchewan where western farmers were given the opportunity of discussing the legislation.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, I think there is a responsibility on members to make sure that the bill is understood. I do not ask members opposite to sell the bill if they do not think it is in their political interests to do so. I think they have an obligation, however, and the government and farmers of this country can ask them to live up to that obligation, to provide producers in their area with the same kind of factual information that was provided in at least one constituency in Saskatchewan.
I see my time is coming to an end, Mr. Speaker, and I do not want to belabour the point any further. We have had a good discussion. I hope the sense of optimism that I expressed earlier will not be misplaced as we come to what I hope will be the conclusion of this important and interesting debate on Bill C-41.
I want to share with the House the experience I have had with this legislation over the past year in the west. Two points are crystal clear as result of the effort at explanation, consultation, and discussion with farmers. First of all there is a broad base, a genuine support for this bill among western grain farmers, and secondly the legislation is far better known and understood by farmers than hon. members opposite would have us believe.
I think it is important to keep in mind the context in which the bill has come forward, not a context of ad hocery or piecemeal changes, but a context of important and ongoing upgrading of the grain industry in western Canada under the leadership of this particular minister for the past four or five years. It is a record of accomplishment. All members associated with the minister, particularly members on the government side, can be very pleased to acknowledge and support that record. One of the main pillars of it is the Western Grain Stabilization Act. I am sure it will stand in the history of this country as a tribute to the foresight and accomplishment of the present minister responsible for the Canadian Wheat Board for his work on behalf of the western grains industry.

Madam Speaker, hon. members now in the Chamber are such nice fellows that I will continue my remarks in a mild vein until the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board and the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) return. In view of the remarks they were making before six o'clock, I hope they get here. They are not the type who fire their guns and then run. I am confident they will be here before my time is up. I hope they do not return just two minutes before I complete my remarks as that would not give me time to say all I want to say to their faces.
I will dwell on some items to convince members opposite to persuade the minister in charge of the wheat board to send this bill back to committee where some fundamental changes can be made in order that this will be a real grain income stabilization program.
As a minimum, the legislation would have to be amended to allow the grain producer to show as a cost of production what farmers all across Canada are allowed to show on their income tax returns under the present federal agricultural stabilization legislation for other farm products. Costs of production legally and properly determined by provincial governments, universities, and experts who compile farm production costs all include farm costs that are excluded from this legislation.
The minister in charge of the wheat board and the hon. member for Assiniboia complain about this bill not being passed quickly. I do not know how they can complain when items that are included in other legislation brought in by a Liberal government are excluded from this bill. I find that passing strange. I hope members opposite will persuade the minister to send the bill back to committee in order that clause 8 may be amended to allow the appropriate costs of production to be included.
There are several things wrong with the legislation. No bill is perfect no matter what government of what political stripe introduces it. It is, of course, the duty of opposition members as well as of organizations and individuals out-

side government to persuade it to make changes which they feel necessary in light of their experience and knowledge. There has been a great deal of difficulty trying to do that with this bill.
I remind hon. members that while the grain stabilization bill is supposed to take into account costs of production, it leaves out certain areas. Statistics compiled within the past few days show that farm costs have risen as well as farm prices. According to these statistics, farm costs have risen in excess of farm prices. Therefore a grain stabilization bill based on costs of production that leave out some of these increased costs is unfair to farmers.
In 1975, including the period of time when the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Macdonald) were telling us to show restraint and stating that they were going to control prices and incomes, farm costs rose in a manner that in fact negated what seemed to be the good price grain producers were getting for wheat, oats, barley, rye, flax and rapeseed.
The cost of farm fuels increased 20 per cent in 1975 over
1974.	Tools, hardware and repairs increased by 20 per cent and hired custom work increased by 20 per cent. Fertilizer went up in price between 25 and 50 per cent in 1975 over 1974, and chemical and sprays increased from 15 to 22 per cent.
Interest charges are specifically excluded from the legislation. Any businessman or farmer of any other product under the Agricultural Marketing Act can show interest charges on machinery, equipment, and buildings as a legitimate cost of production. However, that item is excluded from the grain stabilization bill. Farmers in the rural part of my constituency of Regina-Lake Centre pay from $500 to $3,000 a year in interest charges on farm machinery, equipment, and buildings. That is not included as a legitimate cost of production in this legislation. The minister in charge of the wheat board complains that the opposition is obstructing and delaying this bill. If you were raising any other kind of farm product, then under any other stabilization bill those charges would be considered a legitimate cost of production. Yet they are not included in the legislation before us. The minister in charge of the wheat board, the hon. member for Assiniboia, and the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley (Mr. Mclsaac) were all here during the debate but none of them have answered that question yet.
The minister in charge of the wheat board should be very happy that my hon. friend should have introduced the amendment to third reading which would allow him to speak again and answer that question. In the event, he has refused to answer during the 14 months since the bill was presented for first reading. He refuses to answer because he cannot answer.
Here is another item. When you buy an insurance policy to insure farm buildings or anything else, the cost of that insurance is a legitimate cost of production. Nevertheless, it is excluded under the terms of the bill before us. The minister, the hon. member for Assiniboia, and the hon. member for Battleford-Kindersley have yet to deal with that question. There is a further item-depreciation of farm equipment, farm buildings, and farm machinery. This
January 26, 1976

is an important matter for anyone engaged in farming, primary production or business, yet it is excluded as a legitimate cost of production under the bill we are now considering.
In any year when there is a pay-out under this grain stabilization bill, that pay-out is based on the net tax flow after deduction for the cost of production. If you exclude interest charges, depreciation, and premiums on the stabilization plan you put a fair hole in the credit a grain producer should receive for his cost of production. I should like to ask any hon. member on the government side who comes from a constituency with some farmers in it, in Ontario, Quebec or the Atlantic provinces, to tell me the answer to this question: how come these things form part of the cost of production in your province but are excluded in Alberta, Saskatchewan, Manitoba or the Peace River district of British Columbia?
I want to be perfectly honest with the government members tonight. The hon. member for Brant (Mr. Blackburn) moved the third reading amendment not only because he felt legitimate concern about what this bill contains but because we wanted the minister or the hon. member for Assiniboia to have an opportunity to tell us about the items which had been left out. They have yet to do it.

If we are interested in trying to save the government money, and as a result the taxpayers of Canada, then it seems logical that this program definitely should be operated by the crop insurance commissions because they have their head offices in the three prairie provinces. In addition, in each of these provinces there are district offices established. I do not know just how many district offices there are in the province of Saskatchewan, but I know that in the province of Alberta there are 52 district offices. It seems to me that whatever governmental proceedings have to take place could take place and be controlled out of those offices.
Further, in view of the fact that in a great many cases elevator agents collect for the crop insurance program, so could these same government agencies collect for the stabilization bill, which has to be done. However, there is one significant difference-the crop insurance commissions pay those elevator agents for collecting those fees, but there is no provision in this bill for any payment whatsoever to the elevator agents.
I think that it will not be too far into the future when elevator agents will ask to be reimbursed for this extra work, and rightly so. I think they should be. There is a certain amount of responsibility associated with the collection of this money, especially when public funds are being dealt with. If the government really wants to be fair and wants to operate the plan the way the majority of the producers would like to have it operated, then I am satisfied this is the way this program should be administered, instead of setting up another head office. This would do away with much confusion, and it would help a great deal in communication between the two bodies. As the crop insurance inspectors go out into the country they could do the same work as the inspectors under the grain stabilization plan.
