For a long time I thought that the Minister of Transport wrote his speeches but I have come to the conclusion that it probably works the other way. And I would advise the Minister of Transport to use the speeches that somebody else prepares for him because he does not add to his stature at all by the remarks he made this afternoon.
This is an important piece of legislation, Madam Speaker. It is important for us to look at the question of stabilizing the price of grain, and for the minister to criticize members who feel there should be a different way of providing that stabilization seems to me to be arrogant-a Prussian like attitude. It is not in keeping with the objects of a minister who avows that his interest is in providing a reasonable living for the farmers.
I listened very carefully to the hon. member for Assiniboia; incidentally I think he should be the minister in charge of the wheat board if it is to be separated from the Department of Agriculture. This is probably one occasion when I would support the idea of a second minister in a department. Agricultural stabilization certainly does not belong with Transport; it should come under the Department of Agriculture. There would be some merit in having the hon. member for Assiniboia handle this particular legislation. I say that because his remarks showed his knowledge of the vast detail in this bill, and his understanding that there probably can be a difference of opinion as to how the legislation will apply, and why there is a philosophical difference amongst members on how stabilization should be operated.
In moving the amendment today to refer this bill back to committee for further study my colleagues are talking about two separate things. One is a disagreement that we have in relation to the cost of production figures which are allowed under the bill. They do not allow a number of inputs that are in the agricultural stabilization bill which was introduced last year by the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan). They do not allow interest or premiums paid out through the grain stabilization bill, nor do they allow for the normal depreciation that is considered as part of the normal cost of production.
Those members on the government side who are on the agricultural committee would be well advised to remember

the discussion we had last year on marketing legislation covering various foods and the allowances made for input costs of eggs as opposed to milk. In each case a different formula was being used, and in fact the formula is different from one province to another in many cases.
What we are suggesting is that the formula is spelled out in such detail that it would take a mathematician to understand it. I should like to know where the hon. member for Assiniboia got these three people who were going out to advise the farmers who phoned in with questions how much they would be allowed under certain circumstances after they knew their net proceeds of the previous year. I do not think you would get that kind of answer from the income tax people who were involved in the cost factors that go into the net return versus the gross return and the allowable costs in those returns. I think it would be very difficult to take the figures and tables in this bill and relate them to specific cases.
If we agreed with the first proposition that everything is spelled out and that they are correct, the hon. member for Assiniboia would still have difficulty applying that argument to the second proposition we referred back to the committee. That proposition is that the individual decision will be made in terms of clauses 9, 10 and 11 which take the western area and put it into one area, and which say that under certain circumstances everybody in that area is going to get a payment.
The hon. member for Regina-Lake Centre (Mr. Benjamin) made the point that if this applied in any other universal program where it involved those who were in need and those who were not, there would be considerable complaint from those with less left wing tendencies than from some of us because of the unfairness of the program. It was pointed out that if you had a year in which the criteria were met and the pay-out was made on a broad basis covering a large number of areas-and it is a fact that areas in western Canada have not consistently produced the same ratio of crops as has another area, either in grades or quantities-you would find some people who had a bumper crop being paid out according to their contribution in the same manner as those who had very bad crops for several years. Even if the latter were in a majority and had made little contribution to the program, their benefits coming out of it would be small.
I know that is difficult to understand, Madam Speaker, and I know the farmers are having difficulty understanding it because nobody could be that stupid-except the Minister of Transport. No one else could be that stupid. They would know, because they would talk to the farmers, that crops failures through weather, pestilence, loss of markets or any other consideration that a farmer faces, do not happen uniformly over the three prairie provinces. They do not happen uniformly in one prairie province. I do not come from the prairie provinces but I dare say in each there are at least five zones with totally different weather conditions, different growth, different production abilities, and a number of other factors about which I know nothing.
I know that different factors must be considered, that farmers can get more for Durum wheat than for some other kinds, and that people in the Palliser triangle grow No. 1
January 26, 1976

Northern which is as good as or even better than any wheat grown on the prairies. I know this, and I do not come from the prairies; but the Minister of Transport does not know it, obviously, since he has not provided for this legislation to be applied in different zones.
We are not only asking for the legislation to be applied in zones; we want it applied on an individual basis. We are concerned about the farmers. As for the minister, he has been in his ivory law tower teaching law to people in Saskatchewan. In Saskatchewan they must have produced some lousy lawyers. If he is as bad at law as he is at agriculture, he must be a really bad lawyer. I feel sorry for the people he taught at university.
Every western member who is the least bit honest will admit that there have been crop disasters, but the crop failure has often affected people in one half of a township and not in the other half. Sometimes in one half of a township hail will totally destroy a crop, but the crop in the other part of the township will be unaffected. That is how the good Lord works. He does not always hail out an entire township. But the Minister of Transport thinks that if there is hail in western Canada, it will hail all across the three prairie provinces and that there will be a total disaster in the entire area. He does not realize that it could hail in one half of a township, or in Assiniboia, and not hail at all in an adjacent riding-perhaps because the people of Assiniboia voted differently in the past. But political considerations do not influence the Lord overmuch. When there is a natural disaster, there is no easy way to decide boundaries.
In the committee we suggested boundaries on an individual basis. The minister said no. We suggested township boundaries. The minister said no. Then we suggested that there should be zones within the provinces. Again he said no. In the end we suggested boundaries involving at least the five areas under Wheat Board jurisdiction, which will include the three prairie provinces, part of British Columbia, and part of Ontario, which should be given consideration. But the minister said no, the area of jurisdiction had to be all prairie provinces as one unit.
I suggest that the hon. member for Assiniboia must have spent an awfully long time in school, or somewhere else, because if he had talked to farmers instead of lecturing them he would have discovered that there is a need to break down jurisdictional areas into small parcels if you are to make reasonable and economical payments. As the bill now stands, if the entire crop of the Palliser area is destroyed, say, or there is no market for No. 1 Northern and the whole area suffers a net loss, the result could be large payments to people who had a large income and small payments to people who made a small income.
We have been considering stabilization for some time. Ever since coming here the minister has tried to sell the idea of stabilization, but he knows little about it. His officials know little about it, too. When the committee late last year discussed the agricultural stabilization legislation, it suggested a number of changes. Actually I proposed one motion. We suggested that grains now coming under Canadian Wheat Board jurisdiction should be included as named commodities under the agricultural stabilization bill. We could treat such grains in the same way as we are to treat eight or nine, I think, other commodities. Doing it
Grain Stabilization
this way would mean that we should consider the production of each individual farmer; individual loss of income would be readily discernible, on the basis of which we could make a payment with the help of a subsidy from the federal government.
Obviously the minister relies on the long-term cycles affecting the production of cereal grains. In the near future we can expect reasonably good crops. Really, we need only worry about price on the international and domestic markets, so that the minister is not anticipating a pay-out in the immediate future. Actually if this program had been in force for some time, the last sizable pay-out would have taken place in 1962. True, grain prices were depressed that year, but production costs were not as high as at present. This program could be in existence for some time before conditions arise leading to a pay-out.
More than any other minister, the Minister of Transport has built up his own civil service. It is not our civil service, Mr. Speaker; it is his. He reminds me of Jimmy Gardiner, when Jimmy Gardiner was still a household word. Mr. Gardiner built up an empire including inspectors of diseased sheep and inspectors of just about everything else. I mention the sheep, because he was caught on that matter. The people working for him did not work for the government. They were order in council appointees.
How many civil servants will administer this program? The hon. member for Assiniboia suggested that it will be a few. The program will not involve large administrative costs. That may be so, because the Minister of Transport already has working for him a whole lot of order in council appointees. I am sure he will use the people of the grains group, of the transport study group, of the grains council, and PFAA appointees. All these are the minister's Liberal appointees, part of his machine.
We do not expect it will change anything. However, I disagree with the hon. member for Assiniboia who said it will not cost the farmers or the people of Canada. Jimmy Gardiner's machine cost the farmers a great deal. It could not always be calculated. Even though you could not add it all up, it cost a lot. There is no question about that. It would be interesting to hear from some of the old farmers how much it cost them.
These new appointments, even though they are supposed to work for no pay, will cost the farmers a lot. They are so-called dollar a year men. I read Peter Newman's book about a dollar a year man. I would like to go to the right fishing club. I would not mind working for a dollar a year because the expense accounts are so good. Even though the salaries of these men are very low, the expenses are high.
If the government continues to pass this kind of stupid legislation, there will not be any Liberal members from Saskatchewan.
I was interested in hearing the Minister of Transport talk about his new friends in Unifarm. That is a right wing organization. There is no doubt about that. However, I am not sure they are right enough for the Minister of Transport. I am sure there will be a lot of progressives in that organization who will not be influenced.

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
I am aware that the minister spoke to that organization. He was the guest speaker. They probably were polite. Farm people usually are. If you appear to be totally out of the ball park, they just smile and say, poor boy. They do not push it any farther. However, I am sure they did not buy.
This raises another interesting point. We filibustered on the original grain stabilization bill long enough for the courts to get into the act and stop the minister from cheating. That filibuster saved the farmers many millions of dollars. I think an accurate guess would be $400 million to $500 million was saved by killing the original bill. Right away that year we saved them over $100 million. What the people thought about that stabilization bill was certainly reflected in the election at that time. Some farmers were so mad that they took the government to court. I believe the matter was settled out of court. It was certainly dropped.
The government was cheating by not making the $15 million payment the law said it had to make. The minister wanted to get that through right away. He introduced retroactive legislation to cover the illegality. We held it up by filibustering. We make no apology. We filibustered until the court was able to make a decision. When the minister knew what the court's decision was going to be, the bill was withdrawn and there was no more talk about it.
I am sure that almost everyone in this House supports income stabilization. However, it must be an honest stabilization. We want it to be related to the costs of production. I agree that it will involve quotas and the government having to sell what is produced. It will involve producing as much as possible on the acreage that is allowed. The farmer will agree to do that in the most efficient manner at the lowest cost. He has already agreed to it with regard to a number of other commodities under the stabilization act.
This is a new field. One type of agriculture is being separated from the other areas of agriculture and is being placed under the Department of Transport. The former Minister of Transport should not be offended because this is really not part of the transport field. It is just that the minister responsible for the wheat board now happens to be Minister of Transport.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: I wish Marchand had the wheat board.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
We would rather that anybody else had it instead of having the wheat board follow one minister around. In many ways it is fortunate that there are only three Liberals elected in that province. As I said before, I would rather the wheat board were handled by an associated minister than traipsing around on somebody's caboose where it is being bumped around in a way that it does not deserve.
We are all interested in stabilizing agriculture, but it must be done fairly. It must be the kind of program the individual farmer can afford. It should be related to a number of other programs that we now have, one of which is the agricultural products stabilization board. It has a set of criteria that has worked satisfactorily for the past 20 years. It has its ups and downs but it works relatively well. There are many commodities that producers would like under the Agricultural Stabilization Act. I believe it could apply to grains produced in the prairie provinces as it now applies to wheat produced in Ontario.

There is nothing wrong with the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) having some responsibility for wheat. However, I do not understand why he is not supposed to have anything to do with western wheat.
Production costs differ in various parts of the prairies. Input costs, wheather conditions, soil conditions and production costs per acre differ: There should be an allowance for those differences. That is being taken into consideration in the farm crop insurance programs in which the provinces are involved.
Part of this program is a bastardization of the agricultural products marketing legislation and the crop insurance program. It is neither fish nor fowl in terms of insurance or marketing legislation. Before the\ farmers start making large demands on this program we must be sure that it is the type of program they can live with and is one that will bring some form of income stabilization to western Canada over a long period of time. Any other type of program is only for the political ego of the minister who introduced it.
The minister has not particularly tried to sell this program. There are very few farmers in favour of it and very few opposed to it. They are not opposed for a very simple reason. Initially the minister allowed them to check out of the program. If they go back into the program they can check out for the second time, but not get into it on any additional occasion. They can really check out of the program twice. For this reason no one is particularly opposed to it. However, we are going to spend money on it. I do not care how much money we shall spend on administration. I do not care how much money the minister will require to provide staff in the various agencies under his control to administer this scheme.
Whatever the costs of administration may be, the country as a whole has an interest in this program. Even if no farmers decide to participate there will still be the cost of administration, and I think hon. members would be very foolish to pass a piece of legislation which farmers do not desire to be passed. I have received no letters in the past two years either in support of this program or against it. Hon. members may suggest that I get no letters on the subject because I do not come from Western Canada. May I say, though that I got hundreds of letters about the previous piece of legislation, Bill C-171, in opposition to that particular measure.
It is important that legislation should be either opposed or supported by those it will affect, and there is no evidence of any support for or opposition to this legislation. Thus it seems to me we have failed to provide legislation which will achieve any reasonable result in terms of ensuring a guaranteed income for western farmers.
Western farmers are not particularly interested in insuring against disaster this year. They are not interested because they have already had a good crop. They have had a series of good crops. They have been able to buy new machines, including heavy machinery which enables them to cut down labour costs. They will be paying for those machines for the next eight or ten years, and so long as they receive a reasonable price for their grain and can grow a reasonable grade they will not be complaining very much.
January 26, 1976

I believe the minister now responsible for the wheat board had a personal interest in this legislation which is not in keeping with the opinion expressed this afternoon by the hon. member for Assiniboia who believes sincerely though incorrectly, that this type of legislation is good for the farmers in his area. I suggest that if it is good for the farmers in his area where they are farming light land and grow very good crops in good years, though in other years they may well encounter difficulties, they might find that the same program will not apply in northern Saskatchewan. If he knows this he should consider referring the bill back to the committee to give members a chance to consider regionalization for a second time.

speakerposition: Deputy Speaker and Chair of Committees of the Whole of the House of Commons
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: Order.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, while we are dealing tonight with western grain, more particularly with western wheat, we are dealing with an export commodity, a commodity which is traded internationally on a global basis.
I believe there is something happening out there in the world of which the government is not aware. For the first time in the history of the grain trade all the components are in the system on a world-wide basis. China and Russia are now regular purchasers. Every country has apparently made a decision not to allow its people to starve. So, for the first time, all the components are in the system on a world-wide basis.
Surely before we get into a complicated scheme such as this which is before us tonight, we should have answers to some simple questions. For instance, I have tried to find out from the government how much it costs to produce a bushel of wheat and I cannot get an answer. The government has no figures showing how one deals with the cost of land. I heard the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Goodale) talk about the great record of achievement of the present minister in charge of the wheat board. Look at the government's own figures. According to the Wheat Review we find that the peak export year for Canadian wheat and wheat flour was 1962-63 when the figure was 594 million bushels. In 1972-73, ten years later, we exported 575 million bushels. This year, up until January 14, exports of wheat and Durum combined amounted to 216.1 million bushels. If everything goes well for the balance of the crop year exports of wheat and wheat flour may reach 450 million bushels, which is a far cry from the almost 600 million bushels we exported back in 1962-63.
What about our competitors? What about our great neighbour to the south? Exports of wheat and feed grain from the United States are constantly rising while Canadian exports are declining. Here are some figures. In 1963-64, a good year for Canada, we exported 15 million metric tons. In 1972-73 we exported 15.6 million metric tons. In 1974-75 the figure was 11.2 million metric tons and the projection for next year is 13 million metric tons. Compare these figures with those of our chief competitor, the United States-23 million metric tons in 1963-64, 31.8 million in 72-73, and 28 million in 1974-75. The projection for next year is 36.5 million metric tons.
What is the world import situation? In the year 1963-64, total imports amounted to 57.4 million metric tons. For the present year they are estimated to be 75.8 million metric
Grain Stabilization
tons. Trade in wheat and wheat flour is continuously increasing, yet our exports are likely to be far below the figure of 1963-64.
There is no question that if this bill passes Canada will be subsidizing wheat production in Western Canada. The hon. member for Assiniboia, appearing before the Senate Committee on Agriculture on December 16, had this to say:

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
For last year, just to put a figure on it, had the plan been in place-and this involves some presumptions about participation, crop volumes, prices and this sort of thing-the federal payment into the stabilization fund would have been something in the order of $90 million.
It is obvious to me that if Canada continues to follow the route of stabilization subsidy programs it will lead to an ever-increasing border limitation problem with the United States and the European Economic Community. What we need are long term contracts such as our competitors are entering into with Poland, Russia, and Japan-three and five year contracts. Maybe we should be devoting more attention to setting up a national food bank in this country. I suggest we should spend a little more on market promotion.
It bothers me that this year Canada is going to end up with about a $5 billion trade deficit. Grain exports from this country alone bring in some $3 billion of foreign exchange, and the government wants to tamper with this. I close by saying that with this bill I think we are walking down an unknown road.

speechtext: It is another delay and obstruction move on the part of my hon. friends opposite. speechtext: We will buy that.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
Again earlier this month the Manitoba Farm Bureau-I am not talking of the Palliser wheat group mentioned by some hon. members opposite but the Western Agricultural Conference and the groups that they represent, a very broad representative group of grain producers-sent a telegram to the government, the minister, and to the Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Stanfield), and I suspect hon. members of the NDP as well,

January 26, 1976
Grain Stabilization
urging members of parliament to get busy and pass this legislation.
I do not mind at all giving my hon. friends opposite all the time they require to debate this legislation. Over the years I have been listening to the same old arguments being put forward by my hon. friend from Regina-Lake Centre, the very same arguments he used when he was an organizer in the province of Saskatchewan.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: It seems they were successful anyway.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
I would have expected from him more up-to-date arguments, such as those just put forward by the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek (Mr. Hamilton). His suggestions were at least new and looked to the future. In moving this amendment this evening I think members of the NDP really wanted another chance to villify the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. That has really been the gist of their speeches so far. They have put forward no reason for deferring the legislation by referring it back to committee. They continue to heap abuse upon the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. I do not blame the NDP for finding some excuse for getting up and talking about farm policy because they really do not have a farm policy other than to villify and to criticize the minister. That has been their policy for some time, and again they are making the same old speeches.
It has been interesting to listen to some of the arguments that have been put forward. Some good arguments have been made and they have not all been a waste of time. Some good valid objections have been put forward as well as some very invalid objections. In general we have had a long, protracted debate since the bill was brought in, but the debate has been productive.
This bill, or a version of it, has been before the House and western farmers for almost five years, yet we still hear members opposite saying that perhaps we would move more slowly, that perhaps we should reconsider it. But again, no real alternative as to whom else we should consult and where else we should inquire has been put forward.
In all the time we have debated the bill and this whole concept of stabilization it took the official opposition, the Conservative party opposite, until December 11, 1975, before it came forward with any sort of concrete counter proposal to this concept of grain stabilization. On that date a definite suggestion was put forward by the hon. member for Qu'Appelle-Moose Mountain (Mr. Hamilton), supported by other speakers from that party.
As I say, Mr. Speaker, some real concerns have been raised and I think resolved in this debate. I think we have improved the legislation. The hon. member for Timiskam-ing (Mr. Peters) said he had not had any mail about this subject for the last two years. Although it is good for Canada that current grain prices are high and markets are good, perhaps part of the difficulty felt by all members of the House in trying to have a comprehensive debate on this issue is that the farmers do not really want to think about the day when grain markets and prices are not as good as they are today. But in the meantime I think they do want this House of Commons to proceed with putting in place some kind of fund or program to cushion the day-if and

when it comes; we all hope it will not even though the course of history indicates it is likely to-when things are not so rosy.
The opposition did not like this particular plan. It seems to me that all we heard in the early stages of this debate was that we need a plan but not this one. We talked to farm groups and all were careful to support the principle of stabilization without specifically criticizing what was wrong with this plan, and more particularly without any firm proposal of their own being made until just before Christmas when, after some four or five years, the Conservative party put forward a kind of individual plan. If I had a criticism to make of it, their plan is a great deal more complicated than the one in this bill, and one criticism of this bill has been that its terms are too complicated and detailed.
The NDP-and I give them credit for this-did put forward an alternative, albeit a fairly simple one and a very expensive one. They suggested a fully guaranteed income for all farmers, whether they be grain farmers or some other kind of farmer, whether the farmers needed or deserved it, whether they were good producers, tried hard or made good judgments, or otherwise.
The fact of the matter is that if they had talked to producers in the prairie region, certainly to the grain growers, they would have discovered that even the supporters of the NDP do not want this kind of plan. They may be socialists in other respects and for other reasons, but they do not want the kind of plan that will bonus everyone regardless of whether they do a good job or a poor job of farming. Such a proposal for solving the problems of the grain farmer would not get support.
I do not suggest that the plan embodied in Bill C-41 is perfect. I suspect we will be considering amendments to it once the plan is in operation. But we do need the plan in place. I suggest that opposition delays in the past year have cost the western grain producers millions of dollars because the fund was not in place and building itself up toward the day when that particular plan was in operation.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: Your own minister delayed the bill, and you know it.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
I want to deal with some of the points that have been put forward in this debate. Who wants it? I think we have settled that particular question. All political parties and farm groups are almost unanimous that we do need an income plan of this kind. Although people have expressed concern and criticized this particular bill and some of its complexities, at least they are all there, written into the legislation. It is all there written in, and is not subject to the vagaries of orders in council or changes in that respect.
The program does not provide for pay-outs to the larger grain producers. Some implication was expressed by the hon. member for Yorkton-Melville (Mr. Nystrom) about the 2 per cent for everybody which would be taken out, but the larger producers would not get larger payments because there is that limit to 2 per cent of sales up to a value of $25,000. It may be, of course, that the limit should
January 26, 1976

be raised, but it certainly will not let someone with $100,000 in sales draw out large payments.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: That is a minor detail.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
I do not think it is a minor detail, but it is rather ridiculous to compare this to the unemployment insurance program, medicare, or anything else of that kind.
I have one criticism of the legislation in that it excludes the feed grain producer who chooses to feed his grain to his own livestock. If a barley producer markets his grain to another feed lot, sells it to a feed mill or to the Canadian Wheat Board for export or shipment to eastern Canada and hauls it to the elevator for that reason, he can contribute to the plan and be a part of it, and thereby draw benefits. On the other hand, if that feed grain producer feeds his own livestock he is not able to participate. It seems to me this is an omission in this legislation.
The theory is, of course, that such a producer will be able to benefit from livestock stabilization programs. That might be the fact, but I do not see that we should deny him the right to be a participant in this particular program, because he is a grain producer just the same as the other chap who grows barley and sells it to the Canadian Wheat Board.
I am satisfied that before very long we will again have to bring in some amendments to this legislation, particularly after it gets into operation and we hear from the producers themselves. I think it was the hon. member for Moose Jaw (Mr. Neil) who spoke earlier in the debate about the delays in getting this bill into place. It is not to the credit of members opposite that this legislation is going forward at all. They have stalled and played games for many months in spite of the recitations of dates and so on that we have heard from members here tonight.
Nothing has been said about the many amendments and changes we were able to implement in response to some criticisms opposite and some suggestions both in the committee and at the report stage here in the House.
One other point that keeps coming back into the debate from hon. members of the NDP and the Conservative opposition relates to the number of people who will be employed to handle this legislation. That is a nonsense argument and is not borne out by the facts. Indeed time will demonstrate that this is one of the more phoney arguments they have put forward.
Another suggestion I have heard put forward by members opposite is that this program will destroy the crop insurance program, or somehow jeopardize crop insurance.

subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext: Who said that?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Transport
subsubtopic: PROCEEDS FROM THE PRODUCTION AND SALE OF WESTERN GRAIN
speechtext:
I certainly can check back through the speeches, as I am sure the hon. member could, to find out who made that suggestion. In no way will this program jeopardize the crop insurance program. This program is complementary to the crop insurance program.
Any comparisons made between this program in Bill C-41 and the PFAA are not valid either, because this program will hopefully do a better and better job than the PFAA. This program is not in any way comparable to PFAA.
Grain Stabilization
This brings me to the one point raised by hon. members opposite about what we do about the differences in regions. That is a good and valid question. The proposal put forward by the Conservatives would really mean that we are going to ask the government to set up individual retirement plans or bank accounts for individual producers. I find that surprising coming from the Conservative party. Surely there are enough provisions in other programs and in income tax provisions for the farmers to go ahead and make their own plans in that regard. Really this proposal put forward by the Conservative party as a counter proposal to this legislation would see the government setting up individual funds for each of these grain producers. If the producer did not use the fund during his life time he could then sort of retire on it.
On the one hand hon. members in the opposition do not want the government to spend more money, but on the other hand they say we should set up these little retirement funds. I do not think this plan will stand up in any way. Their proposal has no way of triggering payments in order to do the job intended to be done by Bill C-41, that is, stabilizing over-all grain income whenever that income is low.
This is one more of a number of proposals and policies which have been implemented by the minister in charge of the Canadian Wheat Board. I could talk about setting up the grains group. I do not know why members opposite are particularly critical about that, because this certainly set up people in several departments to look into and highlight the grain industry, with the many good results that have come from that. I could also refer to the good job in sales that is being done by the Wheat Board. The national feed grains policy has provided a major improvement in the disorderly marketing situation we had before.
I would agree that no such scheme as we are debating here tonight in Bill C-41 is going to replace good marketing or good marketing practices. Nor is it going to replace good farm practices or good farm management practices. In this respect I certainly agree with earlier remarks of the hon. member for Swift Current-Maple Creek. The best kind of plan is one that involves a minimum of government intervention and government interference, and leaves the operations of the farmers to their own choices. I think this plan does that and I urge all hon. members to support it, and to reject the amendment.

subtopic: TRANSPORT-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND FERRY SERVICE-REQUEST FOR REPORT OF LABOUR-MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE
TRANSPORT-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND FERRY SERVICE-REQUEST FOR REPORT OF LABOUR-MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the question I wish to raise this evening, and I want to thank the hon. members for giving me some assistance in raising it as the first item, has to do with the continuing concern we in Prince Edward Island and I believe the people in Newfoundland have about the problems with regard to the main transportation link with the mainland, the ferry system.
As hon. members will recall, the last time there was a disruption in the ferry service because of the situation on the railroad in August, 1973, some members on all sides sought assurance from the Minister of Labour and the Minister of Transport that the absolutely catastrophic tie-up of the ferry systems of Prince Edward Island and Newfoundland would be dealt with in the time of peace, so-called, between the resolution of that strike and the entering into of new collective bargaining arrangements two years or more hence. At that time I received an undertaking which appears on the record of Hansard at pages 6142 and 6143 of August, 1973. At that time the minister said:
January 26, 1976

... I can answer the hon. member right now by saying yes, we could correct that situation assuredly so that it would never happen again.
He went on to suggest that the solution should be found elsewhere than in compulsory arbitration. Certainly that is a solution with which I would agree, and I am sure many hon. members on all sides would.
Since that time I have carried on a rather lengthy correspondence with provincial and federal ministers, but particularly with the federal minister of transport. My colleague, the hon. member for Malpeque (Mr. MacLean), on December 3 as reported at page 9685 of Hansard, asked the following written question:
Has any agreement been reached or any arrangement made whereby continuous ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the Mainland can be guaranteed, even when labour contracts are being negotiated?
I was somewhat shocked at the answer of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang), which was as follows:
No agreement has been reached nor has any arrangement been made whereby continuous ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the Mainland can be guaranteed at all times, especially during the ice season and during labour disputes.
Obviously with respect to weather conditions or ice certainly I am not one who believes that the Minister of Transport, regardless of what his powers might be, has reached the area of control of ice conditions or has passed beyond human bounds into the supernatural. We know only too well that these are conditions which so far no technology or political know how has overcome. However, with respect to the question of labour disputes, either present or future, I was mightily disturbed to find that the minister had neither arrived at any kind of solution or agreement with the key parties involved, nor did he seem to be aware of the fact that there has been considerable correspondence with his predecessor, or that in fact his predecessor had established a special committee and that the committee, which is known as the Marine East coordinating committee, had held a series of meetings.
Unfortunately these meetings were without a great deal of success, and this is the reason for my pursuing the matter tonight. As a matter of fact, on December 8 as reported at page 9795 of Hansard I indicated in a supplementary to the Minister of Transport that there was the Marine East co-ordinating committee which had been announced by his predecessor, now the Minister of the Environment (Mr. Marchand), a year ago July, and that the committee was to meet in the months of January, May and September and effect continuing communication on potential labour disputes which might result in the termination of a service which vitally affects the economic interests of Prince Edward Island. I asked specifically whether that committee was still operating and when it might be making a report. The Minister of Transport indicated on December 8 that he had not had a report but that he would look into it. Unfortunately to date the minister has not reported either to this House or to me, and I am still in the dark, as are the people of Prince Edward Island.
This comes against the background of a situation where we know we are into the negotiation of new contracts. I understand the negotiations have not produced any positive results. In light of what has been a continuing series
Adjournment Debate
of labour problems, one cannot be as optimistic as one might otherwise hope to be. When we project the possibility of a crisis situation sometime in the next few months, perhaps during a critical period affecting the economic interests of at least one or two provinces of this country, it is critical that now, well in advance of the time when we reach a crisis situation, the ministries responsible-particularly the Ministry of Transport which has a prime responsibility-should have worked out some kind of solution.
Shortly after the situation in August, 1973, I produced one proposal. I will not take the time of the House to go into detail on that proposal, but it was one possible alternative, a double penalty alternative which in effect would have provided a penalty against both union and management, but would not have penalised the public interest and the people of Prince Edward Island.
I direct the attention of the parliamentary secretary to that proposal. I have had no definitive reply from his department or from officials in the Department of Labour. I have had some kind of preliminary reaction from some unions about the proposal, but that is the extent to which there has been any serious examination of that as an alternative. There have been other suggestions. There has been the suggestion of establishing a Crown corporation, which I really do not think would get us much beyond the present dilemma.
Of course it is known to members of the House that the government of Prince Edward Island, realizing the seriousness of the situation, has had in the courts since late 1973 a legal action against the Government of Canada with respect to its own responsibility to maintain continuous transportation to and from Prince Edward Island, even during times of labour disputes.
I think it is high time, therefore, that the minister or his parliamentary secretary indicated to the House exactly what kind of work is being done, and when we can be assured that we are not going to face, for the third time in a decade, the kind of damaging situation that will affect the income, the prospects, and the operation of the social and economic fabric of Prince Edward Island. I would hope that the parliamentary secretary could give us some of that assurance this evening.

speakeroldname: Mr. Ralph E. Goodale (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Transport):
subtopic: TRANSPORT-PRINCE EDWARD ISLAND FERRY SERVICE-REQUEST FOR REPORT OF LABOUR-MANAGEMENT COMMITTEE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am pleased to be able to respond to my hon. friend again this evening. I have had that opportunity on other occasions at this point in the proceedings, and I am always very interested in the arguments he presents and impressed by the way he puts them to the government and the House.
I can assure the hon. member, as other hon. members on this side of the House have done on other occasions, that the government is very concerned with the matter of the substantial losses incurred by people who are innocent bystanders to labour-management disputes and the situations which arise in the course of industrial relations that deprive innocent people of some kind of service which causes them inconvenience at the least and probably much more than that.

January 26, 1976
Adjournment Debate
I should like to help my hon. friend by providing some background and updating on the work of the Marine East co-ordinating committee.
When the hon. member first asked the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) to state what was being done to ensure continuous ferry service between Prince Edward Island and the mainland with regard to disruptions caused by winter ice conditions and labour disputes, I am afraid the wording may have become a bit confused. I am glad that has been straightened out now and that we are not particularly talking about "acts of God" in the insurance sense of the phrase, but really about losses or disruption caused by labour disputes.
With regard to this particular matter of disruptions due to industrial disputes, the original reply by the minister recognized the fact that ferry service employees enjoyed the right to strike and the government would not want to interfere with that right if such action could be avoided.
The hon. member has drawn attention to the existence of the Marine East co-ordinating committee and appears to be under the impression that this group was set up to eliminate strikes in the ferry service. We only wish-and I speak in a general sense-that that could be true in an easy fashion. The committee in question was set up in an effort to reduce the likelihood of strikes developing, and represents an earnest attempt of management and labour to maintain a relationship which would permit them to identify problem areas in advance and nip potential disputes in the bud.
The existence of this committee, with sub-committees in the various ships and terminals, has provided a useful sounding board and has enabled management and labour to defuse several potentially explosive situations. Nevertheless, despite the success of the co-ordinating committee so far in the maintenance of good management labour relations, it must be recognized that this has not eliminated the possibility of strikes in the ferry services, and the government would be reluctant to interfere with that particular right.

subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-FAMILY ALLOWANCE-REASON FOR FAILURE TO FOLLOW PAYMENT METHOD ADOPTED IN FRANCE
SOCIAL SECURITY-FAMILY ALLOWANCE-REASON FOR FAILURE TO FOLLOW PAYMENT METHOD ADOPTED IN FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, one can read at page 10193 of Hansard for December 19, the Friday before the Christmas recess, that I asked the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Mr. Lalonde) if he had considered the system of family allowance payments in France where only those persons below a certain income level are eligible to receive payments, and for what reason would such a system not be introduced in Canada? The minister gave me a short reply referring to the attitude of the opposition.
We are presently, Mr. Speaker, spending some $2 billion a year on family allowances, and 60 per cent of that amount goes to families with incomes over $12,000.
Well over three million families in Canada receive family allowances, including nearly 900,000 families in the province of Quebec. About 40 per cent have only one child, but the figures go all the way up to some 2,000 families which have ten or more children.
[Mr. Goodale.)
A couple with two children earning a taxable income of $10,000 pay over $2,000 in federal taxes. For similar families with taxable incomes of $20,000 and $30,000, the figures are approximately $5,000 and $9,000 respectively. Those three families receive an after tax benefit on their family allowances of approximately $360, $330, and $300 respectively.
Family allowance payments are equivalent to about a quarter of total personal income tax; so that if, for example, payments were restricted to only half the number of families which presently receive them, that is, those with lower incomes, personal taxes could be reduced by about 12 per cent across the board or by such other ways as would give greater relief to those in lower tax brackets.
The Minister of National Health and Welfare tells us that 20 per cent of families receive less than 6 per cent of family income, whereas the highest one-fifth receive about 40 per cent of family income. With these figures in mind we should be very reluctant to remove the indexing of family allowances. Proportionately, the poor are still getting poorer while the rich are getting richer.
We all like to see universal payments. However, in the case of old age pensions the supplement is based on income. It is therefore not illogical to suggest that family allowance payments should be based on need. This is the way it works in France.
The proposals of the minister concerning income security and adequate minimum incomes are based on need. Thus, while one can argue administrative ease in universal payments, there are many examples where the desirable principle of universality is laid aside for economic necessity.
It is a retrograde step in the over-all program of income redistribution to remove the indexing of family allowances. Why not take this opportunity to revise the entire scheme, maintaining indexing, eliminating payments to those who do not need them and, at the same time, either make compensatory tax reductions or reduce the budgetary deficit?
Answering my question on December 19, the minister referred to the attitude of the opposition. Today, with majority government, unanimity is not essential. The present thinking of the government, which is looking for spending cuts, should be redirected toward the program of family allowances. I should like the Minister of National Health and Welfare, or his representative in the House tonight, the parliamentary secretary, to expand on the short answer given to me on December 19.

speakeroldname: Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
subtopic: SOCIAL SECURITY-FAMILY ALLOWANCE-REASON FOR FAILURE TO FOLLOW PAYMENT METHOD ADOPTED IN FRANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, may I thank the hon. member, my colleague, for raising this question in the House on this occasion. We are dealing with one of the costliest programs of the government. The family allowance program, in which Canadian taxpayers are involved in the redistribution of about $2 billion, absorbs nearly 6 per cent of the total federal budget. So it is not unreasonable that questions from my side of the House, or the opposition side, should be raised about the value of this program and its benefits.
Let me say at the outset that the government is firmly Committed to the program as presently constituted. Between 1968 and 1972, years when I was first a member of
January 26, 1976

parliament, the government put forward a proposal for public consideration which would have involved, in effect, putting a ceiling on family allowances so that families with more than $15,000 annual income would not receive payments. I remind hon. members that the proposal was not well received in the country when it was discussed in an active and lively public debate. People with family incomes of $15,000 were quick to point out that they were not well-to-do, and that for them the family allowance was a considerable benefit.
Remember, the family allowance concept recognizes the fact of dependency, the fact that having children involves extra expense. It recognizes the fact that those expenses usually come at a time in life when a family is newly formed. In most cases the couple has been recently married and must meet considerable expenses in setting up the household and launching on life together. Canadians feel that consideration ought to be given to this.
That discussion resulted in a proposal which was adopted and which goes a long way to meeting the position taken by my colleague. That was the proposal that family allowances be subjected to income tax at the full rates. The effect of that taxation is that approximately $600 million of the $2 billion paid is recaptured by the federal treasury in the form of income tax. It can be seen that a policy that costs $2 billion ends up having a net cost of $1,400 million.
At this time the government is not contemplating going any further and taking back any more of the family allowance than it does through the income tax system for those families with higher incomes. But I would like to put this question to the hon. member and those who feel we should go further. What really is the difference between taking back more of the family allowance than we do and reducing the exemption or deduction which we give families under the income tax system in respect of children? The act gives a child deduction. That again recognizes the fact of dependency. I think one can make the same defence of the deduction for children as one can of the family allowance.

subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-MILLHAVEN-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON GASSING AND BEATING OF INMATES
PENITENTIARIES-MILLHAVEN-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON GASSING AND BEATING OF INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on November 21, 1975, I raised the question of the government's policy with respect to an investigation of an incident at Millhaven Penitentiary relating to certain inmates located in the solitary confinement section of that institution. This incident related to alleged gassing and beating of inmates.
At the same time I asked the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) whether or not public hearings were contemplated with respect to the situation at Millhaven and in other penitentiaries across Canada. The Solicitor General indicated that an investigation was contemplated by the Penitentiary Correctional Ombudsman, and in fact that person is now conducting hearings relating to the Millhaven incidents.
The investigation now taking place only serves to highlight the government's lack of any consistent policy with
Adjournment Debate
respect to prison reform, particularly concerning solitary confinement practices and facilities in federal penitentiaries across the country. The attitude of the government and the Solicitor General in this area, as in many others, is simply to approach each incident with the well-known local brush fire approach to penal reform rather than coming to grips with the fundamental root causes of the problem.
In the first report of the Correctional Ombudsman in July, 1974, Miss Hansen asked for a special study of the use of dissociation in federal prisons, complaining that solitary confinement as a punishment is both cruel and unevenly applied across the country. Recently, Mr. Justice D. V. Heald of the Federal Court of Canada in a judgment described the use of solitary confinement at the British Columbia Penitentiary as cruel and unusual punishment, contrary to the Canadian Bill of Rights.
Why does the Solicitor General therefore not immediately declare the government's intentions with respect to prison reform? If the government is sincerely interested in reform, why does it delay in having the fullest possible public inquiry into the conditions in the federal penal institutions? Is it the government's intention to introduce legislation concerning this matter? Is it not reasonable to ensure that the fullest possible representations on this topic are received?
I note that there is apparently evidence before the Hansen investigation that attempts to form prisoner's committees to voice prisoner's concerns and recommendations for improvement and reform were met by the transfer of committee members to other institutions and the placing of others in solitary confinement.
In conclusion, the Solicitor General owes it to the House and the country to give us a clear and unequivocal statement on these issues, to table the report on solitary confinement, to reply to the Federal Court judgment respecting penitentiary conditions in solitary confinement, and to let us know whether the government has any plans in the area of prison reform to avoid further or more serious incidents than that experienced at Millhaven on November 3 last.

speakeroldname: Mr. Hugh Poulin (Parliamentary Secretary to Solicitor General):
subtopic: PENITENTIARIES-MILLHAVEN-REQUEST FOR REPORT ON GASSING AND BEATING OF INMATES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, before addressing myself to the original question asked in the House on November 21 last, may I make some brief comments.
The concern of the Solicitor General (Mr. Allmand) has been expressed in this House and across the land on numerous occasions. He is interested in prison reform, reform in the nature of establishing penitentiaries of a much smaller size designed to hold between 100 and 150 inmates, instead of 450. The Solicitor General has been trying to establish such institutions so that there might be closer contact, closer supervision, and better means of rehabilitating prisoners, The hon. member mentioned committees of prisoners in penitentiaries. I have met some of these committees in company with the Solicitor General, and as long as they conduct themselves in a meaningful manner their views are listened to and referred to the proper authorities for action.
With respect to the specific incident the hon. member mentioned as occurring on November 3, 1975, this incident

January 26, 1976
Adjournment Debate
happened at the Millhaven institution when tear gas was used to pacify some rebellious and noisy inmates in one area of the dissociation ranges. I might say that many of those who are in these dissociation ranges are there for their own protection, though others are there for disciplinary purposes.
The incident was reported to the Commissioner of Penitentiaries and an administrative inquiry was convened. On November 4, 1975, the correctional officer at the time of the incident was suspended from duty pending the completion of the administrative inquiry. This senior officer was reinstated on duty on November 13, 1975. Disciplinary charges have been laid against him, heard at the institutional level, and referred to the regional director's office for decision. This administrative inquiry revealed facts which were not known on November 3 and 4, 1975. In the light of these new facts, the Solicitor General has requested the correctional investigator, Miss Inger Hansen, to undertake an inquiry into the new facts. This inquiry commenced on January 19 last.
The terms of reference of the inquiry are as follows:
1.	The events leading up to the use of gas and force in the cell range G-l and the environment control area of Mill-haven institution on November 3, 1975, as well as the events following the said use of gas and force, and whether the directives, instruction and standing orders which pertain to the use of gas and force were followed.
2.	Make suggestions with a view to improving the directives, instructions, and standing orders which pertain to the use of gas and force, and/or the way in which such directives, instructions, and standing orders are used.
I am not at present in a position to give the House a full report of the occurrence. That will have to wait until Miss Hansen completes her report. However, I can say that as a result of these incidents some 70 inmates who were in dissociation at the Millhaven institution have been transferred to the Regional Reception Centre, (Ontario), the Collins Bay institution or the Joyceville institution so as to allow the institutional authority to free some correctional officers to maintain the normal activities and programs of the institution since some correctional officers had withdrawn their services on an overtime basis.
